The kernel’s behavior and exploit mitigation features can be tuned during initialization using kernel command-line arguments in /etc/default/grub:
# Add to GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT in /etc/default/grub
GRUB_CMDLINE_LINUX_DEFAULT="quiet splash slab_nomerge init_on_alloc=1 init_on_free=1 page_alloc.shuffle=1 pti=on module.sig_enforce=1 lockdown=confidentiality"

Exploit Mitigation Kernel Flags







Parameter
Defensive Mechanism




slab_nomerge
Prevents merging of kernel slab caches with similar sizes, hindering heap-overflow exploitation across different kernel structures


init_on_alloc=1
Zeros allocated heap and page memory upon allocation, mitigating use-of-uninitialized-memory bugs


init_on_free=1
Zeros memory pages upon free, preventing sensitive data retention and use-after-free data leaks


page_alloc.shuffle=1
Randomizes page allocator freelists, increasing entropy against return-oriented programming (ROP)


pti=on
Enforces Page Table Isolation unconditionally, protecting against speculative execution side-channel attacks


module.sig_enforce=1
Rejects any kernel module lacking a valid cryptographic signature matching the kernel’s trusted keyring


lockdown=confidentiality
Blocks userspace from reading or modifying kernel memory via /dev/mem, /dev/kmem, and debugfs



After updating /etc/default/grub, execute sudo update-grub and reboot the machine to apply the mitigations.

title: Chapter 3: Boot, Initialization, and Runtime Environment
text:
Systemd and Service Security
systemd is the init system and service manager on all major enterprise Linux distributions. While historically criticized for complexity, modern systemd includes a rich declarative sandboxing framework that allows administrators to strictly isolate daemons without writing custom C wrappers.

Key Systemd Security Directives
A hardened systemd unit file (or override drop-in) isolates services using Linux namespaces, cgroups, and capabilities:
# /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service.d/override.conf
[Service]
# Execute with an unprivileged, dynamically allocated user
DynamicUser=yes
User=myapp
Group=myapp

# Filesystem Isolation
ProtectSystem=strict
ProtectHome=yes
PrivateTmp=yes
ReadWritePaths=/var/lib/myapp /var/log/myapp

# Kernel and Device Protection
ProtectKernelTunables=yes
ProtectKernelModules=yes
ProtectKernelLogs=yes
ProtectControlGroups=yes
PrivateDevices=yes

# Privilege and Syscall Restrictions
NoNewPrivileges=yes
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
RestrictAddressFamilies=AF_INET AF_INET6 AF_UNIX
RestrictNamespaces=yes
RestrictRealtime=yes
MemoryDenyWriteExecute=yes
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallFilter=~@privileged @resources @obsolete


Auditing Services with systemd-analyze security
systemd includes a built-in automated security auditor that inspects unit definitions and calculates an exposure score from 0.0 (safest) to 10.0 (exposed):
# Audit the security score of a service unit
systemd-analyze security myapp.service
→ Overall exposure level for myapp.service: 1.2 OK 🙂
  ...
  ✓ ProtectSystem=strict               Service has strict read-only /usr, /boot, /etc
  ✓ NoNewPrivileges=yes                Service cannot acquire new privileges
  ✓ PrivateTmp=yes                     Service has private /tmp and /var/tmp

title: Chapter 3: Boot, Initialization, and Runtime Environment
text:
Shared Libraries and Dynamic Linking
When an ELF binary executes in Linux, the kernel loads the executable and invokes the dynamic linker (/lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2). The linker resolves external symbols by scanning directories listed in the binary’s DT_RUNPATH, environment variables, and /etc/ld.so.cache.

The /etc/ld.so.preload Threat Vector
The file /etc/ld.so.preload allows administrators (or rootkits) to specify shared libraries that are injected into every single dynamically linked process launched on the system. Adversaries frequently write malicious user-mode rootkits into /etc/ld.so.preload to hook functions like readdir(), open(), and pam_authenticate(), hiding malicious files and bypassing logins.
# Verify that ld.so.preload does not exist or is completely empty
ls -la /etc/ld.so.preload

# Ensure /etc/ld.so.conf and /etc/ld.so.conf.d/ are strictly root-writable
sudo chmod 0644 /etc/ld.so.conf
sudo chmod -R 0644 /etc/ld.so.conf.d/


Binary Hardening Flags: RPATH vs RUNPATH
Avoid compiling software with insecure hardcoded library paths (RPATH). Use RUNPATH, and ensure compiling includes stack protection and Read-Only Relocations (RELRO):
# Check binary hardening features with checksec
checksec --file=/usr/bin/ssh
# RELRO: Full RELRO | Stack: Canary found | NX: NX enabled | PIE: PIE enabled

title: Chapter 3: Boot, Initialization, and Runtime Environment
section: Package Management and Software Supply Chain
text:
Package Management and Software Supply Chain
Linux distributions maintain signed package repositories verified via public-key cryptography.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                     PACKAGE SIGNATURE VERIFICATION                     │
│                                                                        │
│   Package Maintainer ──► Signs Release Index with GPG Private Key      │
│                                   │                                    │
│                                   ▼                                    │
│   Distribution Mirror ──► InRelease / Release.gpg                      │
│                                   │                                    │
│                                   ▼ Downloaded by apt / dnf            │
│   Local Machine: /etc/apt/trusted.gpg.d/ ──► GPG Public Key            │
│   Verification: Matches signature? Yes ──► Install package             │
│                                    No  ──► Abort transaction          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Modern GPG Key Storage: Legacy practices stored trusted keys directly in the global keyring /etc/apt/trusted.gpg. Modern distributions require placing armored keys into /etc/apt/keyrings/ and binding them strictly to individual repository sources via the signed-by directive in /etc/apt/sources.list.d/.
Preventing Dependency Confusion: Restrict third-party PPAs and external mirrors. Unvetted repositories can push malicious packages with inflated version numbers (epoch:999) that overwrite core system utilities.

title: Chapter 3: Boot, Initialization, and Runtime Environment
text:
Configuration Drift and System Integrity
Over time, administrative changes, hotfixes, and unauthorized edits cause host configurations to drift away from the secure baseline.

File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) with AIDE
Advanced Intrusion Detection Environment (AIDE) builds an encrypted cryptographic database of file attributes (SHA-256 hashes, inodes, permissions, timestamps):
# Install and initialize AIDE database
sudo apt install -y aide
sudo aideinit

# Move baseline database to active production location
sudo cp /var/lib/aide/aide.db.new /var/lib/aide/aide.db

# Perform manual integrity audit
sudo aide --check


Integrity Measurement Architecture (IMA) and EVM
For high-assurance deployments, the Linux kernel includes IMA and Extended Verification Module (EVM). IMA measures file hashes before execution and stores the measurements in the TPM chip (PCR 10). If an executable’s hash does not match an approved cryptographic signature signed by the enterprise PKI, the kernel blocks execution with EPERM.

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
Identity and access management is the gateway to Linux administration. An attacker who compromises valid credentials or exploits a flaw in authentication mechanisms bypasses network perimeters and lands directly in an authenticated session.
This chapter establishes a robust identity, authentication, and privilege-delegation framework. We examine secure user account lifecycle management, password hashing and aging policies, the Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM) architecture, production OpenSSH server hardening, controlled sudo delegation, multi-factor authentication (MFA), and service account compartmentalization.

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
section: User and Group Administration for Security
text:
User and Group Administration for Security
Default user provisioning frequently creates unnecessary accounts and grants excessive permissions. Secure user lifecycle management adheres to the following principles:

Unique Identity Enforcement: Every human operator must possess an individual account with a unique UID. Shared accounts (e.g., sharing the ubuntu or root account among multiple team members) eliminate non-repudiation and prevent reliable auditing.
Explicit Shell Restrictions: Service accounts that run background daemons must never possess interactive login shells. Assign them /usr/sbin/nologin or /bin/false:
# Create a dedicated, unprivileged system user without an interactive shell
sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin -d /var/lib/worker -M -c "Background Worker" worker
Locking Inactive and Unused Accounts: Stale accounts represent dormant vectors for exploitation. Lock unused default distribution accounts:
# Lock password and expire account
sudo passwd -l daemon
sudo chage -E 0 daemon

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
Password Policy and Credential Security
When password authentication cannot be eliminated entirely, passwords must be protected using modern hashing algorithms and complexity constraints.

Modern Password Hashing (yescrypt & SHA-512)
Legacy hashing algorithms like MD5 ($1$) and DES are completely obsolete and can be brute-forced in seconds using consumer GPUs. Modern enterprise distributions default to yescrypt ($y$) or SHA-512 ($6$):
# /etc/pam.d/common-password
password  [success=1 default=ignore]  pam_unix.so obscure yescrypt rounds=11


Enforcing Quality with pam_pwquality
Configure minimum password complexity requirements in /etc/security/pwquality.conf:
# /etc/security/pwquality.conf
# Minimum password length
minlen = 14
# Require at least one uppercase letter
ucredit = -1
# Require at least one lowercase letter
lcredit = -1
# Require at least one digit
dcredit = -1
# Require at least one special character
ocredit = -1
# Reject passwords with consecutive repeated characters
maxrepeat = 3
# Enforce dictionary check
dictcheck = 1


Password Aging in /etc/login.defs
Control credential lifespans globally in /etc/login.defs:
PASS_MAX_DAYS   90
PASS_MIN_DAYS   7
PASS_WARN_AGE   14

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
Pluggable Authentication Modules (PAM)
PAM is the dynamic framework that handles authentication, authorization, credential management, and session setup across all Linux login services (SSH, local consoles, GUI display managers, sudo).
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        THE PAM STACK ARCHITECTURE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Application (e.g., sshd, sudo, login)                                │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ calls pam_authenticate()                                    │
│   PAM Configuration Layer (/etc/pam.d/<service>)                       │
│          ├─► auth      (Verify identity: password, token, biometrics)  │
│          ├─► account   (Validate account status: expiration, time)     │
│          ├─► password  (Update authentication tokens / hashes)         │
│          └─► session   (Prepare environment: mounts, limits, motd)     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

PAM Control Flags
Each module inside a PAM service stack is governed by a control flag that dictates execution flow:

required: The module must succeed. If it fails, the stack continues executing subsequent modules to obscure which check failed, but access is ultimately denied.
requisite: The module must succeed. If it fails, the stack terminates immediately and denies access.
sufficient: If the module succeeds and no previous required module failed, the stack succeeds immediately without evaluating subsequent modules.
optional: Success or failure is ignored unless it is the only module in the stack.



Hardening Example: Enforcing Account Lockout with pam_faillock
Protect against brute-force password guessing by locking accounts after repeated authentication failures:
# Add to /etc/pam.d/common-auth
auth    required    pam_faillock.so preauth silent audit deny=5 unlock_time=900
auth    [success=1 default=bad] pam_unix.so
auth    [default=die] pam_faillock.so authfail audit deny=5 unlock_time=900
auth    sufficient  pam_faillock.so authsucc
# View and unlock locked accounts
sudo faillock --user alice
sudo faillock --user alice --reset

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
SSH: Secure Remote Administration
The OpenSSH daemon (sshd) is the primary administrative entry point into Linux infrastructure. A hardened sshd_config eliminates legacy cryptographic algorithms, prevents credential abuse, and enforces strict operational boundaries.
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/99-hardened-sshd.conf

# Protocol and Port
Port 22
Protocol 2

# Authentication Constraints
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
PermitEmptyPasswords no
PubkeyAuthentication yes
AuthenticationMethods publickey

# Limit Authentication Attempts
MaxAuthTries 3
MaxSessions 4
LoginGraceTime 30

# Disable Insecure Forwarding by Default
AllowAgentForwarding no
AllowTcpForwarding no
X11Forwarding no

# Idle Timeout (Terminate unresponsive sessions after 15 minutes)
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 3

# Modern, Post-Quantum & Resilient Cryptography
KexAlgorithms sntrup761x25519-sha512@openssh.com,curve25519-sha256,diffie-hellman-group16-sha512
Ciphers chacha20-poly1305@openssh.com,aes256-gcm@openssh.com
MACs hmac-sha2-512-etm@openssh.com

# Whitelist Allowed Administrative Groups
AllowGroups wheel sudo ssh-admins
After modifying the configuration, validate syntax before restarting the daemon:
sudo sshd -t
sudo systemctl reload ssh

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
Sudo and Privilege Escalation Control
The sudo utility enables granular privilege delegation without sharing the root password. However, misconfigured sudoers rules are one of the most common vectors for privilege escalation.

Best Practices for /etc/sudoers

Never edit /etc/sudoers directly with a normal editor: Always use visudo, which validates syntax and locks the file against race conditions.
Use Modular Drop-Ins: Place site-specific rules in /etc/sudoers.d/, ensuring files are mode 0440.
Avoid Wildcard Matching (*): Path wildcards allow users to bypass restrictions via directory traversal (../) or flags.
Disable Dangerous Shell Escapes: Restrict utilities that have built-in shell escape features (e.g., vi, less, awk, find):
# INSECURE: Grants instant root via ':!/bin/bash' inside vi
alice ALL=(ALL) /usr/bin/vi /etc/nginx/nginx.conf

# SECURE: Use sudoedit to edit files without granting binary execution
alice ALL=(ALL) sudoedit /etc/nginx/nginx.conf
Log All Sudo Invocations:
Defaults log_input, log_output
Defaults logfile="/var/log/sudo.log"

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
Multi-Factor Authentication Integration
For high-security bastion hosts and production management nodes, passwords or SSH keys alone should be paired with Time-based One-Time Passwords (TOTP) or hardware tokens (FIDO2/YubiKey).
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        SSH MULTI-FACTOR FLOW                           │
│                                                                        │
│   SSH Client ──► 1. Present Ed25519 Public Key ──► sshd verifies       │
│                                                          │             │
│                                                          ▼ OK          │
│   SSH Client ◄── 2. Prompt: "Enter TOTP verification code"            │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼                                                             │
│   Operator inputs 6-digit code ──► pam_google_authenticator verifies   │
│                                                          │             │
│                                                          ▼ OK          │
│                                                    Session Granted     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Configuring TOTP with Google Authenticator PAM

Install PAM TOTP module:
sudo apt install -y libpam-google-authenticator
Initialize TOTP for the user account:
google-authenticator -t -d -f -r 3 -R 30 -W
Configure PAM for SSH in /etc/pam.d/sshd:
# Add at the top of /etc/pam.d/sshd
auth required pam_google_authenticator.so nullok
Enable multi-factor authentication in /etc/ssh/sshd_config:
KbdInteractiveAuthentication yes
AuthenticationMethods publickey,keyboard-interactive

title: Chapter 4: Identity, Authentication, and Access Control
text:
Service Accounts and Privilege Separation
Daemons and automated background jobs must operate with strictly minimal privileges:

Unique UID/GID per Service: Never group multiple services under a common user (e.g., running both Apache and custom Python scripts under www-data).
No Login and No Password: Ensure passwd -S <user> indicates L (locked) or NP (no password).
Dedicated Directory Boundaries: Restrict service account ownership to specific paths under /var/lib/<service>, /etc/<service>, and /run/<service>. Set directory permissions to 0750 or 0700 to prevent other local accounts from inspecting data or sockets.

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
text:
Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
Persistent storage is the primary repository of enterprise value and the ultimate objective of unauthorized intruders. If an attacker gains local access, weak filesystem mount options, unencrypted block devices, permissive access control lists, or unprotected temporary directories allow rapid data exfiltration, tampering, and privilege escalation.
This chapter establishes end-to-end data protection at rest and in transit through the Linux filesystem hierarchy. We cover defensive mount options, POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs), Linux extended attributes, full-disk encryption with LUKS2 and TPM2 auto-unlock, secure secrets storage, temporary directory protection, removable media defense with USBGuard, and tamper-evident backup patterns.

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
text:
Filesystem Security and Mount Options
Storage volumes should not be mounted with default, permissive options. The Linux VFS layer provides mount flags that neutralize common privilege escalation vectors directly at the filesystem boundary:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        DEFENSIVE MOUNT FLAGS                           │
│                                                                        │
│   Flag        Security Guarantee                                       │
│   ──────────  ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│   nosuid      Ignores SUID and SGID bits. Executables run with caller's│
│               privileges even if file has 4755 permissions.           │
│   noexec      Blocks execution of binary code directly from volume.    │
│   nodev       Prevents interpretation of character or block devices.   │
│   ro          Mounts filesystem as strictly read-only.                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Partitioning Strategy and Recommended /etc/fstab Options
Separating system partitions prevents a denial-of-service attack (e.g., filling /var/log or /tmp) from crashing root (/):
# /etc/fstab hardened mount options

# Dedicated /tmp partition: no devices, no SUID binaries, no executable scripts
tmpfs                   /tmp            tmpfs   defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec,mode=1777,size=2G  0 0

# Shared memory /dev/shm
tmpfs                   /dev/shm        tmpfs   defaults,nodev,nosuid,noexec                    0 0

# /var/tmp: Bound to /tmp or mounted with identical restrictions
/tmp                    /var/tmp        none    bind,nodev,nosuid,noexec                        0 0

# Dedicated /home partition: prevent users from creating device nodes or SUID root tools
UUID=1234-abcd-...      /home           ext4    defaults,nodev,nosuid                           0 2

# Read-only boot partition (remount rw only during kernel updates)
UUID=5678-efgh-...      /boot           ext4    defaults,nodev,nosuid,ro                        0 2

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
section: Access Control Lists and Extended Attributes
text:
Access Control Lists and Extended Attributes
Standard POSIX permissions (owner:group:others) are often too coarse for multi-tenant enterprise applications where multiple disparate services require distinct read or write access to shared datasets.

POSIX Access Control Lists (ACLs)
ACLs allow administrators to attach fine-grained permissions to files and directories for specific users and groups without altering the primary ownership:
# Grant user 'auditor' read-only access to /var/log/audit/
sudo setfacl -m u:auditor:r-x /var/log/audit/

# Grant group 'developers' read-write access to a shared directory
sudo setfacl -m g:developers:rwx /opt/project/data/

# Set default ACLs so all future files created inherit the permissions
sudo setfacl -d -m g:developers:rwx /opt/project/data/

# Inspect effective ACLs
getfacl /opt/project/data/


Extended Attributes and Immutability (chattr)
Extended filesystem attributes (supported on ext4, XFS, and Btrfs) enforce controls that even root cannot bypass without explicitly removing the attribute:

Immutable (+i): The file cannot be modified, deleted, renamed, or linked to. Even root cannot edit an immutable file.
Append-Only (+a): Data can only be appended to the file; existing contents cannot be truncated, overwritten, or deleted. Ideal for security log files.

# Make audit log append-only so an attacker cannot erase traces
sudo chattr +a /var/log/audit/audit.log

# Protect critical configuration file from tampering
sudo chattr +i /etc/resolv.conf

# View extended attributes
lsattr /var/log/audit/audit.log /etc/resolv.conf

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
text:
Disk Encryption with LUKS
Data at rest must be protected against physical theft, decommissioned drive leakage, and hypervisor storage snapshot exfiltration. LUKS2 (Linux Unified Key Setup version 2) is the Linux standard for block-level encryption using dm-crypt.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        LUKS2 ENCRYPTION TOPOLOGY                       │
│                                                                        │
│   Filesystem Layer: ext4 / XFS (Files, directories, inodes)            │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼                                                             │
│   Decrypted Device Mapper: /dev/mapper/cryptroot                       │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ AES-XTS-256 Symmetric Decryption (Hardware AES-NI)          │
│   Encrypted Physical Partition: /dev/nvme0n1p3 (LUKS2 Container)       │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Unlocks via:                                                │
│   ┌───────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Key Slot 0: Passphrase / Keyfile  │ Key Slot 1: TPM2 (PCR 0+7) │   │
│   └───────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Formatting and Opening a LUKS2 Volume
# Format volume with AES-XTS-256 and Argon2id key derivation
sudo cryptsetup luksFormat --type luks2 --cipher aes-xts-plain64 --key-size 512 --hash sha512 /dev/nvme0n1p3

# Open encrypted volume and map to decrypted device
sudo cryptsetup open /dev/nvme0n1p3 cryptroot

# Create filesystem on decrypted device
sudo mkfs.ext4 /dev/mapper/cryptroot


TPM2 Hardware Binding with systemd-cryptenroll
To enable secure, headless boot without embedding plaintext keys on disk, bind the LUKS2 volume to the system’s TPM 2.0 chip, sealed to Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs) 0 (firmware) and 7 (Secure Boot state):
# Enroll TPM 2.0 with PCR 0 and 7 measurements
sudo systemd-cryptenroll --tpm2-device=auto --tpm2-pcrs=0+7 /dev/nvme0n1p3

# Update /etc/crypttab for automatic boot unlocking
# cryptroot  UUID=...  none  tpm2-device=auto
If the firmware is modified or Secure Boot is tampered with, the TPM refuses to release the decryption key, preventing the machine from booting.

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
text:
Secrets and Configuration File Protection
API keys, database credentials, TLS private keys, and environment tokens must be handled with extreme care:

Strict File Permissions: Secrets files must be owned by the target service user with mode 0400 or 0600:
sudo chown myapp:myapp /etc/myapp/secrets.env
sudo chmod 0400 /etc/myapp/secrets.env
Volatile Memory Storage (tmpfs): Store runtime decryption keys in memory-backed filesystems (tmpfs) rather than writing them to persistent disks, ensuring they disappear upon system power-off:
sudo mount -t tmpfs -o size=64M,mode=0700,nodev,nosuid,noexec tmpfs /run/secrets/
Linux Kernel Keyrings: Utilize the kernel keyring facility (keyctl) to store cryptographic keys inside kernel memory rather than exposing them in process environment variables (/proc/$PID/environ), which are readable by other processes sharing the UID.

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
section: Temporary Files and Sensitive Data Handling
text:
Temporary Files and Sensitive Data Handling
The /tmp and /var/tmp directories have historically been fertile ground for symlink attacks, race conditions, and temporary data leakage.

Kernel Hardlink and Symlink Restrictions
Modern Linux kernels include protection against symlink and hardlink spoofing attacks where an attacker tricks a root process into overwriting arbitrary system files:
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-filesystem-security.conf
fs.protected_symlinks = 1
fs.protected_hardlinks = 1
fs.protected_fifos = 2
fs.protected_regular = 2

fs.protected_symlinks = 1: Disallows following symlinks in world-writable sticky directories unless the owner of the symlink matches the owner of the target file or the directory.
fs.protected_hardlinks = 1: Disallows creating hardlinks to files the user does not personally own or have write access to.

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
text:
Removable Media Security
Plugging an unauthorized USB storage device into a physical server presents immediate risks: BadUSB firmware spoofing, malicious HID keyboard injections, and data exfiltration.

Disabling USB Storage via Kernel Module Blacklist
# Blacklist usb-storage driver
cat << 'EOF' | sudo tee /etc/modprobe.d/disable-usb-storage.conf
blacklist usb-storage
install usb-storage /bin/true
EOF


Enforcing Granular USB Authorization with USBGuard
For environments requiring selective USB access (e.g., YubiKeys or management consoles), deploy USBGuard:
sudo apt install -y usbguard

# Generate baseline policy authorizing currently connected devices
sudo usbguard generate-policy | sudo tee /etc/usbguard/rules.conf

# Start and enable the service
sudo systemctl enable --now usbguard
Any unknown USB device plugged into the server will be blocked at the kernel driver layer until explicitly authorized by an administrator.

title: Chapter 5: Filesystem Security and Data Protection
text:
Secure Backup and Recovery
A hardening strategy without verifiable backups is incomplete:

Immutable Offsite Storage: Backups must be replicated to immutable, append-only destinations (such as S3 object locks or air-gapped repositories) where even a root compromise on the production server cannot delete historic snapshots.
Client-Side Encryption: Backups must be encrypted before leaving the host using modern tools like Restic or BorgBackup with authenticated encryption (AES-256-GCM or ChaCha20-Poly1305).
Automated Restore Drills: Backups must be tested quarterly through automated spin-up rehearsals. Untested backups are not backups.

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
The network interface is the primary external attack surface of any connected Linux server. From raw packet floods and TCP sequence manipulation to rogue routing announcements, protocol spoofing, and man-in-the-middle interception, exposed hosts face continuous probing from internet-wide scanners and lateral movement attempts from within the internal network.
This chapter constructs a multi-layered network defense. We harden the Linux TCP/IP stack via sysctl parameters, implement stateful packet filtering using modern nftables, examine enterprise firewall orchestration, enforce system-wide TLS 1.3 cryptographic policies, secure DNS resolution, address IPv6 attack vectors, and configure encrypted overlay tunnels with WireGuard.

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
section: TCP/IP Stack Security and Sysctl Controls
text:
TCP/IP Stack Security and Sysctl Controls
The Linux kernel networking stack contains dozens of tunable knobs exposed via /proc/sys/net/. Default distribution configurations are tuned for maximum interoperability across noisy legacy networks rather than security.
Create a hardened network profile in /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf:
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-network-security.conf

# 1. Defend Against SYN Flood Denial of Service
net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies = 1
net.ipv4.tcp_syn_retries = 3
net.ipv4.tcp_synack_retries = 3
net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog = 4096

# 2. Disable IP Source Routing (Prevents attacker-specified routing paths)
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_source_route = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_source_route = 0

# 3. Disable ICMP Redirect Acceptance (Prevents route table poisoning)
net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.all.secure_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.secure_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_redirects = 0

# 4. Disable ICMP Redirect Sending (Host is not a router)
net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects = 0
net.ipv4.conf.default.send_redirects = 0

# 5. Enable Reverse Path Filtering (Mitigates IP address spoofing)
net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter = 1

# 6. Ignore Broadcast ICMP Echo Requests (Mitigates Smurf amplification attacks)
net.ipv4.icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts = 1

# 7. Ignore Bogus ICMP Error Responses
net.ipv4.icmp_ignore_bogus_error_responses = 1

# 8. Log Martians (Packets with impossible source addresses)
net.ipv4.conf.all.log_martians = 1
net.ipv4.conf.default.log_martians = 1

# 9. Disable IP Forwarding (Ensure non-gateway host does not route packets)
net.ipv4.ip_forward = 0
net.ipv6.conf.all.forwarding = 0

# 10. Disable TCP Timestamps (Mitigates system uptime fingerprinting)
net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps = 0
Apply the parameters immediately:
sudo sysctl --system

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
Network Interfaces, Routing, and Segmentation
A secure host should never expose administrative listening sockets to untrusted network segments:

Localhost Binding: Configure application servers, metrics exporters (e.g., Prometheus node_exporter), and internal databases to bind explicitly to 127.0.0.1 or ::1, rather than 0.0.0.0 (all interfaces):
# In postgresql.conf
listen_addresses = 'localhost'
Interface Segregation: Physical and virtual servers in production should maintain at least two dedicated network interfaces:

Management Interface (VLAN / Private Subnet): Handles SSH, Ansible, metrics collection, and administrative backups.
Data Plane Interface (Public / Load Balancer Subnet): Only exposes the application’s public ingress port (e.g., port 443).

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
Firewalls: nftables and iptables
While iptables served as the Linux packet filtering tool for two decades, it suffers from severe architectural limitations: separate binaries for IPv4 and IPv6 (iptables vs ip6tables), inefficient linear rule inspection, and lack of atomic updates.
nftables is the modern Linux kernel packet classification framework. It unifies IPv4, IPv6, ARP, and bridge filtering into a single bytecode-driven engine (nf_tables) with native set lookups and atomic rule commits.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        NFTABLES HOOK ARCHITECTURE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Incoming Packet                                                      │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼                                                             │
│   PREROUTING ──► Routing Decision ──► INPUT ──► Local Process          │
│                                         │                              │
│                                         ▼ (If Forwarding Enabled)      │
│                                      FORWARD                           │
│                                         │                              │
│   Local Process ──► OUTPUT ──► Routing ─┴─► POSTROUTING ──► Wire       │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Complete Hardened nftables Configuration
Below is a production-grade, stateful, default-drop firewall ruleset for a Linux server:
# /etc/nftables.conf
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

table inet filter {
    # Define sets for management IPs and rate limits
    set admin_v4 {
        type ipv4_addr
        flags interval
        elements = { 10.0.0.0/8, 192.168.1.0/24 }
    }

    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority filter; policy drop;

        # 1. Allow traffic on loopback interface
        iif "lo" accept

        # 2. Drop invalid packets immediately
        ct state invalid drop

        # 3. Accept established and related connections (Stateful tracking)
        ct state { established, related } accept

        # 4. Allow essential ICMP / ICMPv6 (Path MTU discovery, ping)
        ip protocol icmp icmp type { echo-request, destination-unreachable, time-exceeded } limit rate 5/second accept
        ip6 nexthdr icmpv6 icmpv6 type { echo-request, destination-unreachable, packet-too-big, time-exceeded, nd-router-advert, nd-neighbor-solicit, nd-neighbor-advert } limit rate 5/second accept

        # 5. Allow SSH only from authorized management CIDRs with rate limiting
        ip saddr @admin_v4 tcp dport 22 ct state new limit rate 10/minute accept

        # 6. Public Ingress: Allow HTTPS (port 443)
        tcp dport 443 ct state new accept

        # 7. Log and drop remaining unsolicited packets
        limit rate 3/minute log prefix "NFT_INPUT_DROP: " flags all
        drop
    }

    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority filter; policy drop;
    }

    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority filter; policy accept;
    }
}
Load and enable the ruleset:
sudo nft -c -f /etc/nftables.conf    # Check syntax
sudo systemctl enable --now nftables
sudo nft list ruleset

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
Firewalld and Policy Management
On Red Hat, Fedora, and SUSE distributions, firewalld acts as a dynamic management daemon that manages nftables underneath.
# View active zone and configured services
sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones
sudo firewall-cmd --zone=public --list-all

# Remove insecure default services
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --remove-service=cockpit
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --remove-service=dhcpv6-client

# Add SSH with rich rule restricting access to internal subnet
sudo firewall-cmd --permanent --zone=public --add-rich-rule='rule family="ipv4" source address="10.20.0.0/16" service name="ssh" accept'

# Reload firewalld to commit changes
sudo firewall-cmd --reload

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
section: TLS, Certificates, and Encryption in Transit

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
DNS Security and Configuration
Plaintext DNS queries (port 53) are vulnerable to interception, manipulation, and cache poisoning.

DNSSEC and DNS-over-TLS with systemd-resolved
Configure systemd-resolved in /etc/systemd/resolved.conf to validate cryptographic DNSSEC signatures and encrypt queries using DNS-over-TLS (DoT):
# /etc/systemd/resolved.conf
[Resolve]
DNS=1.1.1.1#cloudflare-dns.com 9.9.9.9#dns.quad9.net
FallbackDNS=1.0.0.1 149.112.112.112
DNSSEC=yes
DNSOverTLS=opportunistic
MulticastDNS=no
LLMNR=no
sudo systemctl restart systemd-resolved
resolvectl status

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
IPv6 Security Considerations
Many administrators configure strict IPv4 firewalls while inadvertently leaving IPv6 completely unmonitored. Threat actors exploit this asymmetry by scanning for IPv6 link-local or global addresses to bypass IPv4 rules.

Parity Principle: Every firewall rule, rate limit, and monitoring policy applied to IPv4 must be mirrored identically in IPv6.
Rogue Router Advertisements (RA): Malicious hosts on a local subnet can broadcast spoofed ICMPv6 Router Advertisements to re-route outbound host traffic. Mitigate this by disabling RA acceptance on static servers:
net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra = 0
net.ipv6.conf.default.accept_ra = 0
Disabling IPv6: If IPv6 is not routed or supported within your infrastructure, disable it explicitly to eliminate the attack surface:
# In /etc/sysctl.d/99-disable-ipv6.conf
net.ipv6.conf.all.disable_ipv6 = 1
net.ipv6.conf.default.disable_ipv6 = 1
net.ipv6.conf.lo.disable_ipv6 = 1

title: Chapter 6: Network Security Hardening
text:
VPNs and Secure Remote Access
Traditional VPN protocols (IPsec, PPTP) suffer from massive codebases, complex key negotiation phases, and weak default ciphers.

WireGuard: Modern Kernel-Level Cryptographic Routing
WireGuard operates directly in the Linux kernel using state-of-the-art cryptography (Noise protocol framework, Curve25519, ChaCha20-Poly1305, BLAKE2s):
# /etc/wireguard/wg0.conf
[Interface]
Address = 10.100.0.2/24
PrivateKey = <ClientPrivateKey>
ListenPort = 51820

[Peer]
PublicKey = <GatewayPublicKey>
Endpoint = vpn.corp.internal:51820
AllowedIPs = 10.100.0.0/24, 10.0.0.0/8
PersistentKeepalive = 25
WireGuard creates a secure, authenticated, and encrypted network interface (wg0). Because WireGuard does not respond to unauthenticated packets, port scans against its UDP port report closed, providing stealth against automated internet scans.

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
The Linux kernel is the supreme arbiter of execution, memory management, and hardware resource allocation. Because all user-space security controls depend directly on the kernel’s integrity, compromising the kernel represents an instant, total defeat of all security boundaries on the machine.
Over the past decade, kernel developers have engineered sophisticated defensive primitives designed to eliminate memory corruption vulnerabilities, constrain the system call surface, enforce cryptographic module boundaries, and prevent code reuse attacks. This chapter explores these kernel security mechanisms in depth.

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)
Address Space Layout Randomization randomizes the memory locations of program execution regions—the stack, heap, shared library mappings, and executable base address—on each invocation. This prevents attackers from relying on predictable memory offsets when crafting buffer overflow and return-oriented programming (ROP) exploits.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        MEMORY LAYOUT WITH ASLR                         │
│                                                                        │
│   Execution Run A                      Execution Run B                 │
│   ┌───────────────────────────┐        ┌───────────────────────────┐   │
│   │ Stack      (0x7fff42e1...)│        │ Stack      (0x7fff89a4...)│   │
│   ├───────────────────────────┤        ├───────────────────────────┤   │
│   │ Memory Mappings (mmap)    │        │ Memory Mappings (mmap)    │   │
│   │ libc.so    (0x7f83b102...)│        │ libc.so    (0x7f12e450...)│   │
│   ├───────────────────────────┤        ├───────────────────────────┤   │
│   │ Heap       (0x55bc14a0...)│        │ Heap       (0x55ef8821...)│   │
│   ├───────────────────────────┤        ├───────────────────────────┤   │
│   │ Binary     (0x55bc1000...)│        │ Binary     (0x55ef8000...)│   │
│   └───────────────────────────┘        └───────────────────────────┘   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Kernel Virtual Address Space Randomization (kernel.randomize_va_space)
Control userspace ASLR via sysctl:
# Query active ASLR mode
cat /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space

0: Disabled (No randomization).
1: Conservative randomization (Shared libraries, stack, mmap regions).
2: Full randomization (Randomizes data segment/brk heap as well).

Ensure full ASLR is enforced in /etc/sysctl.d/99-kernel-security.conf:
kernel.randomize_va_space = 2


Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization (KASLR)
While userspace ASLR protects applications, KASLR randomizes the base address where the Linux kernel code itself is decompressed and loaded into physical and virtual memory at boot time. To prevent unprivileged users from discovering the kernel’s randomized base offset via debug symbols:
kernel.kptr_restrict = 2
kernel.dmesg_restrict = 1

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Non-Executable Stacks and Memory Protections
Historically, attackers exploited buffer overflows by writing shellcode directly onto the call stack and redirecting the instruction pointer (EIP/RIP) to execute that memory.

The NX / XD Bit (No-Execute / Execute-Disable): Supported by modern CPU MMUs, the NX bit marks pages in the page table as non-executable. The stack, heap, and writable data pages are assigned RW- (read-write, no-execute), while code segments are assigned R-X (read-only, execute).
\(W \oplus X\) (Write XOR Execute): The operating system enforces the invariant that memory pages may be writable or executable, but never both simultaneously. This neutralizes straightforward shellcode injection.

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Control-Flow Integrity and Stack Protection
When an attacker cannot inject new executable code due to NX policies, they execute Return-Oriented Programming (ROP), chaining together small sequences of existing machine instructions ending in a ret instruction (known as gadgets) to hijack program logic.

1. Compiler Stack Canaries
Compiled with -fstack-protector-strong, compilers place a random cryptographic canary value between local buffers and the saved frame pointer/return address on the stack:
┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ [Local Buffer] ──► [Random Canary Value] ──► [Saved Return Address]   │
└───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Before a function executes ret, it compares the canary value against a master thread-local register. If a buffer overflow has corrupted the canary, the glibc runtime terminates the process immediately (*** stack smashing detected ***).


2. Hardware Control-Flow Integrity: Intel CET and ARM BTI

Intel Control-flow Enforcement Technology (CET): Implements hardware Shadow Stacks that store return addresses in an isolated, hardware-protected memory region inaccessible to normal write instructions. Any mismatch between the data stack and shadow stack triggers a control protection fault (#CP).
ARM Branch Target Identification (BTI): Restricts indirect jumps and calls to valid target locations tagged with dedicated bti instructions, thwarting arbitrary gadget chaining.

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Seccomp and System Call Filtering
Secure Computing Mode (seccomp) is the kernel’s mechanism for restricting which system calls a process can issue. A compromised web application or database does not need to mount filesystems, load kernel modules, or alter routing tables.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        SECCOMP-BPF EXECUTION FLOW                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Userspace Process issues syscall (e.g., execve, ptrace)              │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼                                                             │
│   Kernel Seccomp BPF Filter Evaluates Syscall Number & Arguments       │
│          ├─► SECCOMP_RET_ALLOW    ──► Execute syscall normally         │
│          ├─► SECCOMP_RET_ERRNO    ──► Return errno (e.g., EPERM)       │
│          ├─► SECCOMP_RET_LOG      ──► Log to audit and allow           │
│          └─► SECCOMP_RET_KILL     ──► Terminate process immediately    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Using Extended BPF (eBPF) or cBPF filters, seccomp inspects the system call number and its register arguments.

Practical Seccomp Enforcement in Systemd
You do not need to write raw C to enforce seccomp. Modern systemd provides high-level syscall filtering groups:
# In service unit configuration:
[Service]
# Block all dangerous syscalls related to raw memory, module loading, and clocks
SystemCallFilter=@system-service
SystemCallFilter=~@privileged @resources @obsolete @raw-io
SystemCallErrorNumber=EPERM

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Linux Capabilities in Practice
As introduced in Chapter 2, capabilities dissect root into granular privileges. When deploying production daemons:
# Example: Inspect current capabilities bounding set
capsh --print

# Drop all capabilities and retain only CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
sudo /sbin/capsh --drop=cap_sys_admin,cap_sys_rawio,cap_dac_override -- -c "/usr/sbin/myapp"

Ambient Capabilities
For non-root services that need to bind to privileged ports without running as root or setting file xattrs, use systemd’s AmbientCapabilities:
[Service]
User=http-service
Group=http-service
AmbientCapabilities=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE
CapabilityBoundingSet=CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
text:
Kernel Lockdown and Module Signing
Even with root access, a system should prevent arbitrary modification of kernel memory. Kernel Lockdown provides two strict enforcement levels:

Lockdown Integrity (lockdown=integrity): Disables kernel features that allow userspace to modify running kernel code:

Disables /dev/mem, /dev/kmem, and /dev/port.
Restricts hibernation (suspend to disk) to prevent booting tampered images.
Requires all loaded kernel modules to possess valid cryptographic signatures.

Lockdown Confidentiality (lockdown=confidentiality): Subsumes integrity mode and additionally prevents userspace from extracting sensitive cryptographic keys or memory secrets from the kernel:

Blocks raw kernel memory inspection via debugfs and /proc/kcore.
Restricts arbitrary BPF program execution and kernel hardware breakpoint registers.


# Check current lockdown status
cat /sys/kernel/security/lockdown
# [none] integrity confidentiality

Enforcing Cryptographic Kernel Module Signatures
Configure the kernel to unconditionally reject unsigned modules by setting:
# In /etc/default/grub: module.sig_enforce=1
If an attacker compiles a malicious rootkit module (rootkit.ko), insmod fails with Required key not available (ENOKEY).

title: Chapter 7: Kernel Security Mechanisms
section: Kernel Exploit Mitigations and Patch Strategies
text:
Kernel Exploit Mitigations and Patch Strategies
Kernel vulnerabilities occur continuously. A sustainable security posture requires structured patch management:

Kernel Livepatching: Avoids disruptive reboots for critical security vulnerabilities. Canonical Livepatch (Ubuntu) and kpatch (RHEL) apply dynamic function redirections to running kernels without rebooting:
# Check livepatch status on Ubuntu
canonical-livepatch status
Scheduled Reboot Cadence: Livepatching only addresses specific, localized CVEs. When architectural changes or major releases occur, orchestrate node drains and automated rolling reboots.
Restricting Unprivileged eBPF: Unprivileged eBPF has been a persistent source of local privilege escalation. Disable it globally:
kernel.unprivileged_bpf_disabled = 1
net.core.bpf_jit_harden = 2

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
Discretionary Access Control (DAC)—the standard Unix user, group, and permission bit model—suffers from a fatal structural flaw: the owner of a resource completely dictates who can access it, and any process running as root can bypass all DAC checks entirely. If an unprivileged daemon running as root (or compromised via a local exploit) is tricked into reading /etc/shadow or writing to /etc/ld.so.preload, the operating system permits the action without hesitation.
Mandatory Access Control (MAC) solves this vulnerability. Under MAC, the operating system enforces centralized, policy-defined constraints that neither users nor root processes can override. This chapter examines the Linux Security Module (LSM) framework and explores the two premier MAC implementations: SELinux and AppArmor.

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
Mandatory Access Control Fundamentals
In DAC, access decisions depend on the identity of the user and the file’s permission bits. In MAC, every operation is evaluated against an immutable system security policy:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        DAC VS MAC DECISION ENGINE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Discretionary Access Control (DAC)                                   │
│   Process (UID 0 / root) ──► Wants /etc/shadow ──► Allowed immediately │
│                                                                        │
│   Mandatory Access Control (MAC)                                       │
│   Process (httpd_t)      ──► Wants /etc/shadow ──► DENIED BY POLICY   │
│   (Even if process runs with EUID 0, policy forbids httpd_t from       │
│    reading shadow_t objects)                                           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Subjects: Active entities that request operations (processes executing in specific domains or profiles).
Objects: Passive system resources requested by subjects (files, sockets, IPC queues, block devices, memory regions).
The Principle of Strict Containment: A compromised web server process should only be capable of reading web files, writing to its designated log directory, and binding to its assigned TCP port. Even if an attacker executes a shell inside that process, MAC rules prevent the shell from reading user home directories, inspecting other processes, or tampering with system configurations.

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
SELinux Architecture and Policy Models
Developed initially by the United States National Security Agency (NSA) and Red Hat, Security-Enhanced Linux (SELinux) implements Flask architecture via the Linux Security Module (LSM) hooks:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        SELINUX ARCHITECTURE                            │
│                                                                        │
│   Userspace Process (Subject)                                          │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Syscall (e.g., open("/var/www/index.html"))                 │
│   Linux Kernel VFS / DAC Check (Passes)                                │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼                                                             │
│   LSM Hook: selinux_file_open()                                        │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Query Access Vector Cache (AVC)                             │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ AVC (In-Memory Cache): Cached decision?                      │     │
│   │   ├─► YES: Allow or Deny immediately                         │     │
│   │   └─► NO:  Consult Security Policy in Security Server        │     │
│   └──────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘     │
│                                  ▼                                     │
│   Security Server: Evaluates Rule (httpd_t -> httpd_sys_content_t:read)│
│                                  │                                     │
│   Result: Allow ──► Update AVC Cache ──► Complete Syscall              │
│           Deny  ──► Generate Audit Log ──► Return -EACCES              │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The SELinux Context Format
Every process and file in SELinux carries a security context composed of four fields:
\[\text{user} : \text{role} : \text{type} : \text{level}\]
Example file context: system_u:object_r:httpd_sys_content_t:s0

User (system_u): The SELinux user identity.
Role (object_r): The role (used in Role-Based Access Control).
Type (httpd_sys_content_t): The core attribute for Type Enforcement (TE).
Level (s0): Multi-Level Security / Multi-Category Security (MLS/MCS) sensitivity rating.

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
SELinux Configuration and Administration
SELinux operates in one of three modes: 1. Enforcing: Security policy is strictly enforced; unauthorized actions are blocked and logged. 2. Permissive: Unauthorized actions are allowed, but denials are logged to the audit system. Essential for testing and troubleshooting. 3. Disabled: SELinux hooks are completely deactivated in the kernel.
# Query current SELinux status
sestatus

# Temporarily switch between Permissive and Enforcing modes
sudo setenforce 0    # Permissive
sudo setenforce 1    # Enforcing

# Inspect security contexts on files and processes
ls -Z /var/www/html/
ps -eZ | grep nginx

Restoring File Contexts with restorecon
When files are copied or moved, their SELinux types may become mismatched, leading to spurious permission errors. Use restorecon to reset file labels to match the system policy specifications:
# Recursively restore standard contexts according to policy database
sudo restorecon -Rv /var/www/html/

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
SELinux Policy Writing and Customization
When an application requires legitimate access blocked by default policies:

Analyze Denials with ausearch and audit2why:
# Search audit logs for AVC denials
sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent

# Translate cryptic denial messages into human-readable explanations
sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent | audit2why
Generate and Install Custom Policy Modules with audit2allow:
# Generate a type enforcement (.te) draft and compiled module (.pp)
sudo ausearch -m AVC -c "mydaemon" | audit2allow -M mydaemon_policy

# Inspect generated rules before loading!
cat mydaemon_policy.te

# Install the compiled policy module
sudo semodule -i mydaemon_policy.pp

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
AppArmor Architecture and Profiles
AppArmor is the default MAC system in Ubuntu, Debian, and openSUSE. Unlike SELinux’s label-based approach, AppArmor is path-based: it binds security profiles directly to the absolute filesystem path of the executable program (/usr/sbin/nginx).
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        APPARMOR PROFILE STATES                         │
│                                                                        │
│   Profile Mode      Behavior                                           │
│   ────────────      ─────────────────────────────────────────────────  │
│   Enforce           Violations are blocked immediately and logged.     │
│   Complain          Violations are permitted, but logged as warnings.  │
│   Disabled          Profile is unloaded from the kernel.               │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Profiles are defined as human-readable plain text files located in /etc/apparmor.d/.

Anatomy of an AppArmor Profile
# /etc/apparmor.d/usr.sbin.myapp
#include <tunables/global>

/usr/sbin/myapp {
  #include <abstractions/base>
  #include <abstractions/nameservice>

  # Network permissions
  network inet stream,
  network inet6 stream,

  # Capability restrictions (Only allow binding low ports)
  capability net_bind_service,

  # Explicit filesystem access rules
  /usr/sbin/myapp mr,
  /etc/myapp/** r,
  /var/log/myapp/** rw,
  /var/lib/myapp/** rw,
  /run/myapp/myapp.pid rw,

  # Explicitly deny access to sensitive files
  deny /etc/shadow r,
  deny /etc/ssh/** r,
}

r: Read
w: Write
m: Memory map executable
x: Execute

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
AppArmor Configuration and Administration
AppArmor provides simple, interactive utilities for creating, testing, and managing profiles:
# Check loaded profiles and running confined processes
sudo aa-status

# Place a profile in complain mode for testing
sudo aa-complain /usr/sbin/myapp

# Place a profile in strict enforcement mode
sudo aa-enforce /usr/sbin/myapp

# Interactive profile profiling: parse audit logs and generate rule updates
sudo aa-logprof

# Wizard for authoring a new profile from scratch by monitoring execution
sudo aa-genprof /usr/sbin/mydaemon

title: Chapter 8: Mandatory Access Control: SELinux and AppArmor
text:
Choosing Between SELinux and AppArmor
Organizations frequently debate which MAC framework to deploy:








Criterion
SELinux
AppArmor




Primary Distributions
RHEL, Rocky, Alma, Fedora
Ubuntu, Debian, SUSE


Model Type
Label/Type-based (Inodes tagged with xattrs)
Path-based (Bound to executable paths)


Granularity
Extremely fine (System-wide, MLS/MCS, users/roles)
Application-focused, straightforward


Learning Curve
Steep (Complex policy language, debugging tooling)
Gentle (Human-readable rules, simple syntax)


Container Integration
First-class (container_t, automated MCS categories)
Standard profile support via Docker/CRI


Path Rename Robustness
Invariant across file moves or renames
Requires updated path rules if binary moves



Recommendation: Align with your distribution’s upstream standard. Do not attempt to force SELinux onto Ubuntu or AppArmor onto RHEL in production. Both frameworks, when actively running in Enforcing mode, neutralize over 90% of zero-day local privilege escalation and service breakout attacks.

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
text:
Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
Preventative security controls—such as firewalls, file permissions, and Mandatory Access Control—are essential, but they are incomplete without visibility. An adversary operating inside an unmonitored infrastructure will systematically probe for misconfigurations, test privilege escalation vectors, and establish persistence completely unnoticed.
Security monitoring transforms an opaque Linux system into a transparent, auditable environment. This chapter covers the logging and auditing architecture: system logging with journald and rsyslog, the kernel-level Linux Audit framework (auditd), remote log shipping over TLS, File Integrity Monitoring (FIM), host-based intrusion detection, automated compliance scanning with OpenSCAP, and Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) integration.

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
section: System Logging with Journald and Rsyslog
text:
System Logging with Journald and Rsyslog
Linux logging is orchestrated through a partnership between systemd-journald and traditional syslog daemons (such as rsyslog or syslog-ng).
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        LINUX LOGGING ARCHITECTURE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Applications / Kernel / Daemons                                      │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ /dev/log & /run/systemd/journal/socket                      │
│   systemd-journald (Binary, indexed, structured storage)               │
│          │                                                             │
│          ├─► Query locally via: journalctl                             │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ ForwardToSyslog = yes                                       │
│   rsyslog (Rule filtering, plain text formatting)                      │
│          │                                                             │
│          ├─► Local text logs: /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/syslog       │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Remote Encrypted Forwarding (TLS / RELP)                    │
│   Central SIEM / Log Cluster (Elasticsearch, Graylog, Splunk)          │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Hardening systemd-journald
Configure /etc/systemd/journald.conf to enforce persistent, tamper-resistant logging with rate-limit protections:
# /etc/systemd/journald.conf
[Journal]
Storage=persistent
Compress=yes
Seal=yes
RateLimitIntervalSec=30s
RateLimitBurst=10000
MaxRetentionSec=1month
MaxFileSec=1day

Seal=yes: Enables Forward Secure Sealing (FSS), utilizing cryptographic keys to ensure that an attacker who subsequently achieves root access cannot retroactively alter or delete past log entries without detection.



Forwarding Logs Over TLS with Rsyslog
Plaintext syslog over UDP port 514 is unauthenticated and easily intercepted or spoofed. Configure rsyslog to transmit logs over an encrypted mutual-TLS channel in /etc/rsyslog.d/60-remote-tls.conf:
# /etc/rsyslog.d/60-remote-tls.conf
# Certificate and TLS parameters
global(
    DefaultNetstreamDriver="gtls"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverCAFile="/etc/ssl/certs/ca-corp.crt"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverCertFile="/etc/ssl/certs/host.crt"
    DefaultNetstreamDriverKeyFile="/etc/ssl/private/host.key"
)

# Forward all auth and authpriv events to remote SIEM
auth,authpriv.* action(
    type="omfwd"
    target="siem-collector.corp.internal"
    port="6514"
    protocol="tcp"
    StreamDriver="gtls"
    StreamDriverMode="1"
    StreamDriverAuthMode="x509/name"
    StreamDriverPermittedPeers="siem-collector.corp.internal"
)

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
text:
Linux Audit Framework and Auditd
While journald captures application-level output, the Linux Audit Framework operates directly inside the kernel, intercepting system calls before they return to userspace. It provides an incontrovertible record of file modifications, privilege transitions, and system executions.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        KERNEL AUDIT ARCHITECTURE                       │
│                                                                        │
│   Userspace Syscall: unlink("/etc/passwd")                             │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼                                                             │
│   Kernel Syscall Dispatcher ──► Kernel Audit Subsystem (kauditd)       │
│                                           │ Evaluates /etc/audit/rules │
│                                           ▼ Matches Rule               │
│                                 Netlink Socket (NETLINK_AUDIT)         │
│                                           │                            │
│                                           ▼                            │
│                                 auditd Userspace Daemon                │
│                                           │                            │
│                                           ▼ Writes to:                 │
│                                 /var/log/audit/audit.log               │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Hardened Production Audit Rules
Place audit rules in /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules. Group rules by function and tag them with distinct -k keys for fast querying:
# /etc/audit/rules.d/audit.rules

# 1. Self-Defense: Monitor audit configuration and tools
-w /etc/audit/ -p wa -k audit_config
-w /etc/libaudit.conf -p wa -k audit_config
-w /sbin/auditctl -p x -k audit_tools
-w /sbin/auditd -p x -k audit_tools

# 2. Monitor Identity, Authentication, and Passwords
-w /etc/passwd -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/group -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/security/ -p wa -k identity
-w /etc/pam.d/ -p wa -k pam_config

# 3. Monitor Sudo and Privilege Escalation
-w /etc/sudoers -p wa -k sudo_config
-w /etc/sudoers.d/ -p wa -k sudo_config
-w /var/log/sudo.log -p wa -k sudo_actions

# 4. Monitor System Initialization and Systemd Units
-w /etc/systemd/ -p wa -k systemd_units
-w /lib/systemd/system/ -p wa -k systemd_units

# 5. Monitor Network Configuration
-w /etc/network/ -p wa -k network_config
-w /etc/netplan/ -p wa -k network_config
-w /etc/resolv.conf -p wa -k network_config

# 6. Capture Unauthorized File Access Failures (EACCES and EPERM)
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open,openat,creat,truncate -F exit=-EACCES -k access_denied
-a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S open,openat,creat,truncate -F exit=-EPERM -k access_denied

# 7. Make Configuration Immutable (Must be the final rule in the file!)
-e 2

-e 2: Locks the audit configuration. Once set, rules cannot be modified, cleared, or disabled without a complete system reboot.

Load rules and test:
sudo augenrules --load
sudo auditctl -s    # View status


Searching Audit Events with ausearch and aureport
# Search for identity modifications
sudo ausearch -k identity -ts today

# Search for failed access denials
sudo ausearch -k access_denied -ts recent

# Generate summary report of authentication attempts
sudo aureport -au --summary

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
text:
File Integrity Monitoring
File Integrity Monitoring (FIM) detects unauthorized file additions, deletions, and modifications across the system.

AIDE Scheduled Verification
As introduced in Chapter 3, AIDE builds a cryptographic inventory of system files. Automate daily scans and alert on unexpected diffs via systemd timer:
# /etc/systemd/system/aide-check.service
[Unit]
Description=AIDE File Integrity Check

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/aide --check

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
text:
Intrusion Detection and Malware Scanning

Host-Based Intrusion Detection (HIDS) with Wazuh / OSSEC: Wazuh collects system logs, correlates audit events against signature rules, checks for rootkit presence, and detects brute-force attacks in real time.
Rootkit Hunting with rkhunter and chkrootkit:
sudo apt install -y rkhunter
sudo rkhunter --update
sudo rkhunter --propupd    # Baseline system properties
sudo rkhunter --check --skip-keypress

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
text:
Vulnerability and Compliance Scanning
Automated compliance tools verify that thousands of hardening controls match authoritative benchmarks.

OpenSCAP Command-Line Auditing
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) maintains SCAP standards. Use oscap to audit systems against CIS or DISA STIG benchmarks:
sudo apt install -y libopenscap8 scap-security-guide

# Evaluate the host against the CIS Ubuntu Level 2 Server profile
sudo oscap xccdf eval \
  --profile xccdf_org.ssgproject.content_profile_cis_level2_server \
  --results-arf /var/log/compliance/report-arf.xml \
  --report /var/log/compliance/report.html \
  /usr/share/xml/scap/ssg/content/ssg-ubuntu2404-ds.xml
The resulting HTML report gives a clear compliance score and detailed remediation scripts for failed rules.

title: Chapter 9: Auditing, Logging, and Security Monitoring
text:
SIEM Integration and Alerting
Centralizing logs into a SIEM (Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Splunk, or cloud-native tools like AWS CloudWatch and GCP Cloud Logging) allows security operations centers (SOCs) to trigger immediate alerts on critical signals:

Audit Key Alerts: Any event matching -k audit_tools or -k identity triggers an urgent P1 notification.
Root Login Alerts: Any SSH or console session initiated as UID 0 generates an instant security notice.
Rapid Auth Failures: More than 10 failed logins within 60 seconds from a single IP triggers automated IP blocking via fail2ban or nftables dynamic sets.

title: Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
text:
Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
A hardened operating system kernel and strict network perimeter provide little protection if the services running on top are misconfigured. Application workloads—web servers, database engines, mail transfer agents, CI/CD build runners, and cloud bastion hosts—are the interfaces that process external user inputs and business logic.
This chapter details the hardening of common Linux server workloads: web servers and reverse proxies, database management systems, DNS/mail infrastructure, cloud instances and metadata services, CI/CD runners, and distribution-specific maintenance lifecycles.

title: Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
text:
SSH Server Hardening
While Chapter 4 introduced basic SSH identity constraints, production SSH servers require end-to-end operational hardening:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-production-hardening.conf

# 1. Network and Connection Limits
MaxStartups 10:30:100
PerSourceMaxStartups 3
MaxAuthTries 3
LoginGraceTime 20

# 2. Strict Authentication Boundary
PermitRootLogin no
PasswordAuthentication no
ChallengeResponseAuthentication no
KerberosAuthentication no
GSSAPIAuthentication no
PubkeyAuthentication yes

# 3. Disable Environment Forwarding
# Prevents client environment variables (LD_PRELOAD) from infecting the shell
PermitUserEnvironment no

# 4. Restrict Insecure Subsystems
DisableForwarding yes
X11Forwarding no

# 5. Restrict to Specific Users or Groups via Match Blocks
Match Group devops-bastion
    AllowTcpForwarding yes
    AuthorizedKeysFile /etc/ssh/authorized_keys/%u

Rate Limiting and Automated Banning with fail2ban
Install and configure fail2ban to automatically drop brute-force connection attempts at the firewall:
# /etc/fail2ban/jail.d/sshd.local
[sshd]
enabled = true
port = 22
filter = sshd
backend = systemd
maxretry = 3
findtime = 600
bantime = 3600
banaction = nftables-multiport

title: Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
text:
Database Server Security
Databases (such as PostgreSQL and MySQL) house the enterprise’s most critical data assets.

PostgreSQL Hardening Checklist

Network Binding: Bind strictly to internal interfaces or Unix domain sockets:
# /etc/postgresql/16/main/postgresql.conf
listen_addresses = '10.0.10.5, localhost'
Strict Client Authentication (pg_hba.conf): Mandate SCRAM-SHA-256 and reject cleartext or MD5 passwords:
# /etc/postgresql/16/main/pg_hba.conf
# TYPE  DATABASE        USER            ADDRESS                 METHOD
local   all             postgres                                peer
hostssl app_db          app_user        10.0.20.0/24            scram-sha-256
host    all             all             all                     reject
Dedicated Unprivileged Service Account: Ensure the PostgreSQL process runs strictly as user postgres with a umask of 0077, ensuring database data directories (/var/lib/postgresql/data) are inaccessible to other local users.

title: Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
text:
Cloud Instances and Bastion Hosts
Virtual machines deployed in public clouds (AWS EC2, Google Cloud Engine, Azure VMs) operate in specialized networking and identity environments.

Securing the Instance Metadata Service (IMDSv2)
In public cloud environments, instances query a link-local address (169.254.169.254) to fetch IAM role credentials. A Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) flaw in a web application can expose these credentials to an attacker.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        IMDSv2 SESSION ENFORCEMENT                      │
│                                                                        │
│   1. Request Session Token (PUT Request + Hop Limit = 1)               │
│   TOKEN=`curl -X PUT "http://169.254.169.254/latest/api/token" ...`   │
│                                                                        │
│   2. Fetch Metadata with Token                                         │
│   curl -H "X-aws-ec2-metadata-token: $TOKEN" \                         │
│        http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Enforce IMDSv2 unconditionally via AWS CLI or Terraform (http_tokens = "required").
Set the metadata response hop limit to 1 so that containerized workloads or proxies running on the instance cannot reach the metadata service.



Bastion Jump Host Architecture

Do not attach public IP addresses to internal database or application nodes; place them in private subnets.
Access internal subnets strictly through an ephemeral bastion host guarded by SSH certificates, IP whitelisting, and multi-factor authentication.

title: Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
text:
CI/CD Systems and Build Infrastructure
CI/CD runner agents (such as GitLab Runners, GitHub Actions Self-Hosted Runners, Jenkins workers) execute untrusted code from git branches:

Avoid Running Build Agents as Root: Never run runner daemons as root. Use isolated system accounts.
Ephemeral Containers: Execute each build job inside an ephemeral, disposable container destroyed immediately upon job completion.
Avoid Mounting Host Docker Sockets: Mounting /var/run/docker.sock inside a CI build container grants the build job total root access over the host machine. Instead, use rootless build tools (such as kaniko or buildah) that build images entirely in userspace without requiring host privileges.

title: Chapter 10: Secure Service and Workload Configuration
text:
Distribution-Specific Considerations
Enterprise Linux distributions differ in their maintenance cadences, security advisory portals, and long-term support (LTS) mechanisms:

Ubuntu LTS & Ubuntu Pro: Standard Ubuntu releases provide 5 years of maintenance. Ubuntu Pro extends this to 10–12 years with Expanded Security Maintenance (ESM) covering universe packages and kernel livepatches. Monitor Ubuntu Security Notices (USN).
Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL): RHEL delivers 10 years of support with Extended Update Support (EUS) branches. Security errata are categorized as Critical, Important, Moderate, and Low (RHSA).
Automated Security Updates: Enable automated security updates for minor patch releases while maintaining change control:
# Enable unattended-upgrades on Debian/Ubuntu
sudo apt install -y unattended-upgrades
sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades

title: Chapter 11: Container and Virtualization Security
text:
Chapter 11: Container and Virtualization Security
The migration from physical bare-metal hardware to containers and hypervisors transformed infrastructure delivery. However, abstraction layers introduce unique security boundaries and shared-resource risks.
Containers are not lightweight virtual machines; they are ordinary Linux processes executing on a shared host kernel, isolated solely by namespaces, cgroups, seccomp filters, and Linux Security Modules (LSM). Virtual machines provide hardware-enforced hypervisor boundaries, but introduce complex device emulation layers.
This chapter details the mechanisms required to secure containerized and virtualized workloads: container runtime hardening (containerd, Docker), Kubernetes node defense, container image supply chain integrity, hypervisor isolation (KVM, libvirt, sVirt), and defensive analysis of container breakout vectors.

title: Chapter 11: Container and Virtualization Security
text:
Container Security Architecture
To secure containers, one must understand how the container isolation perimeter is constructed in the Linux kernel:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      THE CONTAINER DEFENSE LAYERS                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Application Process (e.g., nodejs, python)                           │
│   ├─ User Identity: Runs as non-root UID 10001 (USER directive)        │
│   │                                                                    │
│   ▼                                                                    │
│   Layer 1: Capabilities & Primitives                                   │
│   ├─ Capability Bounding Set: Stripped of CAP_SYS_ADMIN, CAP_NET_ADMIN │
│   ├─ NoNewPrivileges = true: Blocks setuid execution                   │
│   │                                                                    │
│   ▼                                                                    │
│   Layer 2: Syscall Boundary                                            │
│   └─ Seccomp-BPF Profile: Blocks dangerous syscalls (ptrace, unshare)  │
│   │                                                                    │
│   ▼                                                                    │
│   Layer 3: Mandatory Access Control (LSM)                              │
│   └─ AppArmor / SELinux (sVirt/container_t): Confinements on paths     │
│   │                                                                    │
│   ▼                                                                    │
│   Layer 4: Virtualization & Isolation                                  │
│   └─ Namespaces (mnt, pid, net, ipc, uts, user) & cgroups v2 limits    │
│   │                                                                    │
│   ▼                                                                    │
│   Linux Host Kernel (Ring 0)                                           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
