Every machine code instruction fetched by a CPU core, every network packet buffered by a network interface card, every relational database record cached from NVMe storage, and every thread stack allocated for concurrent tasks exists as a pattern of electrical charges within physical dynamic random-access memory (DRAM).
Yet, no contemporary application software interacts directly with physical memory addresses. If every user-space program had direct, unmediated access to physical memory buses, computing would remain trapped in the fragile paradigm of early microcomputers: a single pointer error in an unprivileged process could overwrite kernel dispatch tables, crashing the entire machine. Furthermore, programs would be statically bound to specific physical memory layouts, making dynamic multitasking, containerization, and safe multi-tenancy fundamentally impossible.
The Linux kernel resolves this tension through one of the most sophisticated, high-performance software subsystems ever engineered: the Virtual Memory (VM) and Memory Management (MM) subsystem.

title: Introduction
section: The Primacy of Memory in Systems Engineering
text:
The Primacy of Memory in Systems Engineering
Virtually every critical performance, reliability, and security incident on modern production Linux servers is rooted in the memory subsystem:

Latency Spikes and Tail Latency: Minor and major page faults, translation lookaside buffer (TLB) shootdowns across hundreds of CPU cores, and direct reclaim stalls under memory pressure create the mysterious p99 latency spikes that plague distributed microservices.
Resource Starvation and Cascading Failures: When available RAM is exhausted, the Linux Out-of-Memory (OOM) killer intervenes. Understanding the heuristics that govern victim selection—and how memory cgroups enforce hard ceilings—is the difference between an isolated container restart and a catastrophic host crash.
Security Boundaries and Exploitation: Over 70% of high-severity software vulnerabilities involve memory corruption: use-after-free (UAF) flaws, buffer overflows, slab out-of-bounds writes, and side-channel microarchitectural leaks (Spectre, Meltdown, MDS). Hardening the memory management layer is the premier defensive priority for systems security.
Hardware Saturation: Modern cloud instances feature multi-terabyte memory configurations distributed across multiple NUMA sockets with high-bandwidth interconnects (AMD Infinity Fabric, Intel UPI). Poor NUMA memory placement degrades throughput by over 40% due to cross-socket interconnect bottlenecks.

title: Introduction
section: Architecture and Mechanics: Why Abstraction Matters
text:
Architecture and Mechanics: Why Abstraction Matters
The Linux memory management subsystem operates across multiple distinct abstraction layers:

Hardware Layer: The Memory Management Unit (MMU), hardware page table walkers, Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLB), cache lines (64-byte coherency protocols), and physical DRAM channels.
Physical Page Management (Buddy Allocator): Manages raw physical page frames (struct page and modern multi-page folios) partitioned across NUMA nodes and memory zones (ZONE_DMA, ZONE_NORMAL, ZONE_MOVABLE).
Object Allocator Layer (SLUB): Eliminates internal fragmentation by carving physical page allocations into small, fixed-size object caches for kernel data structures (struct task_struct, struct inode, struct dentry), utilizing lockless per-CPU caches for maximum multi-core concurrency.
Virtual Memory Architecture: Constructs independent, virtual address spaces for each process, managed via mm_struct and red-black trees / maple trees of vm_area_struct memory regions.
Paging and Reclaim Layer: Coordinates demand paging, Copy-on-Write (COW) page sharing, anonymous memory swapping, LRU scan lists, memory compaction, and the unified VFS page cache.

title: Introduction
section: Scope and Journey of This Guide
text:
Scope and Journey of This Guide
This guide is structured as an end-to-end, deep-dive curriculum spanning 17 progressive chapters and a concluding synthesis:

Chapters 1–3 (Foundations & Translation): Establish physical memory limitations, MMU hardware mechanics, multi-level page table walks by hand, and the Linux virtual address space layout.
Chapters 4–6 (Allocators: Physical, Kernel, and User): Master the Buddy Allocator (mm/page_alloc.c), the modern SLUB allocator, and user-space allocation engines (glibc ptmalloc, jemalloc, tcmalloc) alongside vmalloc.
Chapters 7–10 (Paging, Caching, and Compaction): Explore demand paging page fault handlers, the unified page cache, LRU reclaim loops, compressed zswap caching, and Transparent Huge Pages (THP).
Chapters 11–13 (NUMA, Cgroups, and OOM): Deep dive into enterprise multi-socket NUMA topologies, cgroups v2 memory controllers, and the inner mechanics of the OOM killer.
Chapters 14–17 (Locking, Performance, Security, and Architectures): Dissect memory locking concurrency, eBPF performance profiling, memory exploit mitigations, and cross-architecture differences across x86-64, ARM64, and RISC-V.

Whether you are an SRE troubleshooting high memory pressure in Kubernetes, a systems programmer optimizing database cache locality, a kernel engineer modifying allocation pathways, or an architect sizing high-throughput cloud infrastructure, this text provides the foundational principles and operational tools required to master modern Linux memory engineering.

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
text:
Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
At the lowest physical level, computer memory is a simple, linear array of indexed bytes. In early microcomputers running MS-DOS or early Unix on processors without Memory Management Units (MMUs), application software executed directly against these physical addresses.
While conceptually straightforward, running software directly on bare physical memory imposes devastating structural limitations on multitasking operating systems. This chapter explores why direct physical memory sharing is untenable in modern computing, how virtual memory provides the fundamental illusion of private, contiguous storage, and the overarching design philosophy governing the Linux memory management subsystem.

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
section: The Memory Problem: Why Programs Cannot Share Physical Memory Directly
text:
The Memory Problem: Why Programs Cannot Share Physical Memory Directly
Consider a system where two independent programs—a database server (db_engine) and a web proxy (web_proxy)—execute simultaneously directly on physical RAM without an abstraction layer:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   THE DIRECT PHYSICAL MEMORY FAILURE                   │
│                                                                        │
│   Physical Address Space (0x00000000 to 0x3FFFFFFF - 1 GiB)            │
│  ┌──────────────────────┬──────────────────────┬─────────────────────┐ │
│  │ Operating System     │ db_engine Data       │ web_proxy Stack     │ │
│  │ (0x0000 to 0x1FFF)   │ (0x2000 to 0x5FFF)   │ (0x6000 to 0x8FFF)  │ │
│  └──────────────────────┴──────────────────────┴─────────────────────┘ │
│                               ▲                          │             │
│                               │ Malformed Pointer Write  │             │
│                               └──────────────────────────┘             │
│                 A single out-of-bounds pointer in web_proxy            │
│                 silently corrupts the live state of db_engine!         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Operating directly against physical addresses introduces four fatal problems:

No Spatial Isolation or Protection: Every program can read and write any physical memory address. A bug in an unprivileged web application can overwrite the operating system kernel’s interrupt vector table or inspect another user’s cryptographic private keys in RAM.
Relocation and Address Binding Chaos: Compilers and linkers generate machine instructions with explicit memory references (e.g., JMP 0x00401000). If two different programs are compiled to load at physical address 0x00401000, they cannot run concurrently. The operating system would have to rewrite every absolute pointer in a binary upon loading—a slow, fragile process known as dynamic relocation.
Severe Fragmentation: As processes start, allocate memory, terminate, and exit, physical memory develops holes (external fragmentation). A machine might have 2 GiB of total free RAM scattered across thousands of small, non-contiguous 16 KiB chunks, yet a new process requiring a contiguous 10 MiB buffer would fail to load.
Physical Capacity Ceilings: A program cannot allocate more memory than the physical RAM modules installed on the motherboard. Large datasets cannot be processed without complex, manual application-level disk overlay swapping.

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
section: Virtual Memory as an Abstraction Layer
text:
Virtual Memory as an Abstraction Layer
Virtual Memory resolves these challenges by introducing an indirection layer between the memory addresses referenced by CPU instructions and the physical storage cells inside DRAM chips.
Every process executes within its own private Virtual Address Space. When an application’s thread executes MOV RAX, [0x00007FFF5B290000], the address 0x00007FFF5B290000 is a Virtual Address:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        VIRTUAL ADDRESS TRANSLATION                     │
│                                                                        │
│   Process A: Virtual Address 0x4000 ───┐                               │
│                                        ▼                               │
│                              [Translation Engine]                      │
│                               (Hardware MMU + Page Tables)             │
│                                        │                               │
│   Process B: Virtual Address 0x4000 ───┤                               │
│                                        │                               │
│                                        ▼                               │
│   Physical RAM:                                                        │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ Physical Frame 0x12A000: Mapped to Process A Virtual 0x4000  │     │
│   │ ...                                                          │     │
│   │ Physical Frame 0x9B4000: Mapped to Process B Virtual 0x4000  │     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Both Process A and Process B can read and write to virtual address 0x4000 simultaneously without interference. The hardware translation engine maps Process A’s 0x4000 to physical frame 0x12A000, while mapping Process B’s 0x4000 to a completely distinct physical frame 0x9B4000.

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
text:
Processes, Address Spaces, and Isolation
Virtual memory guarantees process isolation:

Hardware-Enforced Private Sandboxes: A process can only access physical memory frames that are explicitly mapped in its private page tables. Attempting to dereference a virtual address that has no valid mapping triggers a hardware exception that the operating system intercepts as a Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV).
Controlled Sharing: When processes genuinely need to share memory—such as when multiple instances of /usr/bin/bash execute, or when applications link against /lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libc.so—the operating system maps the identical read-only physical code pages into the virtual address spaces of all running processes. RAM is consumed only once.
Predictable Compiling: Every binary can be compiled with the assumption that it owns the entire user-space address space (e.g., canonical low virtual addresses from 0x0000000000400000 up to 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF on x86-64).

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
section: The Role of the Operating System in Memory Management
text:
The Role of the Operating System in Memory Management
While address translation occurs entirely in hardware on every instruction clock cycle, the operating system owns the policies and data structures that configure the hardware:

Creating and Managing Page Tables: The OS allocates the physical memory for page table trees and populates them with physical address translations and permission bits.
Responding to Hardware Page Faults: When a program references an unmapped address, the CPU freezes the executing thread and jumps into the kernel’s page fault interrupt handler. The OS allocates a physical page, loads data from disk if necessary, updates the page tables, and resumes thread execution.
Paging and Eviction: When physical memory nears exhaustion, the OS decides which physical pages should be compressed, written to secondary swap storage, or discarded, reclaiming space for active processes.

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
text:
Hardware Support: MMUs and Protection
Virtual memory cannot be implemented efficiently in software alone. A software emulation layer that intercepted every memory access would degrade execution speed by a factor of 100 or more.
Virtual memory relies on dedicated hardware built into the CPU: - Memory Management Unit (MMU): A dedicated hardware block inside the processor that intercepts all virtual memory references generated by execution pipelines, walks page tables stored in physical RAM, verifies access permissions, and outputs physical addresses onto the hardware memory controller bus. - Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB): An ultra-fast, on-chip associative cache inside the MMU that stores recently resolved virtual-to-physical translations, allowing translation to complete in less than one nanosecond. - Protection Bits: Hardware page table entries store permission flags checked by the MMU on every access: - Read/Write (R/W): Read-only vs read-write permissions. - User/Supervisor (U/S): Ring 3 user-space vs Ring 0 kernel supervisor privilege. - Execute-Disable (NX / XD): Prevents machine code execution from data pages.

title: Chapter 1: Foundations of Memory Abstraction
text:
The Linux Memory Management Philosophy
The Linux memory management subsystem is governed by four foundational engineering principles:

Free Memory Is Wasted Memory: Unused RAM provides zero benefit to computing. Linux aggressively utilizes all idle physical memory as an in-RAM Page Cache to cache disk reads and buffer writes. When applications request memory, the kernel evicts clean cache pages instantly.
Lazy Allocation (Demand Paging): The kernel avoids doing work until the exact microsecond it becomes unavoidable. Calling malloc(1024 * 1024 * 1024) (1 GiB) allocates zero physical bytes of RAM; the kernel merely records the reservation in virtual memory structures. Physical RAM frames are allocated page-by-page only when the application actually writes to the addresses.
Optimism (Memory Overcommit): Because applications routinely allocate far more virtual address space than they ever actively write to, Linux defaults to Overcommit Mode (vm.overcommit_memory = 0), granting virtual allocation requests that exceed the physical capacity of RAM and swap combined.
Locality and Hierarchy: Modern architectures are heavily non-uniform. Linux tunes memory placement to maximize CPU L1/L2/L3 cache hits, minimize TLB misses via huge pages, and prioritize allocating RAM on the local NUMA socket where the calling CPU core resides.

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
text:
Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
Virtual memory operates at the physical boundary where software abstractions meet silicon microarchitecture. While the Linux kernel defines the layout of address spaces, every single instruction fetch and data read must be translated into physical electrical signals across the memory bus in fractions of a nanosecond.
This chapter details the hardware foundations of memory management: Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO), the internal architecture of the Memory Management Unit (MMU), multi-level page table structures, the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB), inter-processor TLB shootdowns, modern x86-64 4-level and 5-level paging, ARM64 and RISC-V translation architectures, memory caching attributes, and a complete worked example of walking an x86-64 page table by hand.

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
text:
Memory-Mapped I/O and Physical Addressing
In modern computer architectures, physical memory addresses do not map solely to physical dynamic RAM (DRAM) chips:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        PHYSICAL ADDRESS SPACE MAP                      │
│                                                                        │
│   0x0000000000000000 ──► Physical RAM (DRAM Bank 0)                    │
│   ...                                                                  │
│   0x000000007FFFFFFF ──► Physical RAM (2 GiB boundary)                 │
│   0x0000000080000000 ──► PCIe MMIO Window (Bar Registers, GPU, NIC)   │
│   ...                    (Writes directly manipulate device registers) │
│   0x00000000FFFFFFFF ──► High BIOS / SPI Flash ROM (Firmware)          │
│   0x0000000100000000 ──► Extended Physical RAM (Upper Banks)           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Physical DRAM: Memory controllers map system DRAM sticks into designated spans of the physical address space.
Memory-Mapped I/O (MMIO): Hardware peripherals (NVMe storage controllers, PCIe network interface cards, GPUs) expose internal control registers and packet buffers as ranges within the physical address map. When the CPU executes a write to an MMIO physical address, the transaction routes across the PCIe root complex rather than DRAM.
Port I/O vs MMIO: While legacy x86 CPUs supported dedicated Port I/O instructions (IN / OUT), modern high-performance devices communicate almost exclusively via MMIO and direct memory access (DMA).

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
text:
The Memory Management Unit Architecture
The Memory Management Unit (MMU) is the hardware component inside the CPU core responsible for translating virtual addresses into physical addresses.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        CPU MMU TRANSLATION PIPELINE                    │
│                                                                        │
│   Instruction Pipeline generates Virtual Address: 0x7FFF50001ABC       │
│                               │                                        │
│                               ▼                                        │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB) Lookup                    │     │
│   │ Check L1 Instruction / Data TLB                              │     │
│   └───────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                               │                                        │
│            ┌──────────────────┴──────────────────┐                     │
│            ▼ TLB Hit (99% of cycles)             ▼ TLB Miss (< 1%)     │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐    ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │
│   │ Physical Address Output      │    │ Hardware Page Table Walker   │ │
│   │ (Latency: ~1 clock cycle)    │    │ Reads CR3 -> PGD -> P4D ->   │ │
│   │                              │    │ PUD -> PMD -> PTE from RAM   │ │
│   │                              │    │ (Latency: 10 - 50 ns)        │ │
│   └──────────────┬───────────────┘    └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │
│                  │                                   │                 │
│                  ▼                                   ▼                 │
│   Memory Controller / L1 Cache Access          Refill TLB and Return   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
When an address cannot be translated—because no page table entry exists or permissions are violated—the MMU halts instruction execution and raises an Interrupt 14 (#PF - Page Fault Exception), saving the faulting virtual address into the CR2 control register and jumping into the kernel’s trap handler.

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
section: Page Tables: Structure, Levels, and Walks
text:
Page Tables: Structure, Levels, and Walks
Why are page tables structured as multi-level trees rather than a simple flat array?
On a 64-bit architecture with standard \(4\text{ KiB}\) pages, a 48-bit virtual address space contains \(2^{36} \approx 68.7\text{ billion pages}\). A flat array mapping 68 billion pages would require:
\[68,719,476,736 \text{ entries} \times 8 \text{ bytes per entry} = 512 \text{ Gigabytes}\]
Every single process on the system would consume 512 GiB of RAM just to store its page table, before storing a single byte of application data!

Multi-Level Trees: Sparsity and Compactness
Multi-level page tables solve this by organizing translations as a sparse B-tree: - Intermediate levels are allocated only when valid memory mappings exist within that branch. - An application using 50 MiB of memory allocates only a handful of intermediate \(4\text{ KiB}\) directory tables, consuming less than 100 KiB of metadata memory.

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
section: Translation Lookaside Buffers and TLB Shootdowns
text:
Translation Lookaside Buffers and TLB Shootdowns
Because traversing a 4-level or 5-level page table requires up to five sequential memory accesses to DRAM (costing 50–100 ns), the MMU relies on the Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB).
The TLB is a tiny, highly associative hardware cache holding the most recent translations: - L1 Data TLB (dTLB): Typically 64 entries; 1-cycle access latency. - L1 Instruction TLB (iTLB): Typically 64–128 entries. - L2 Shared TLB (sTLB): Typically 1,024–2,048 entries; 4–8 cycle latency.

The TLB Shootdown Problem
When the kernel modifies a page table entry (e.g., during munmap(), page migration, or swapping) on a multi-core server, the old virtual-to-physical translation may still be cached inside the private hardware TLBs of dozens of other CPU cores running threads of that process.
To prevent other cores from reading or writing stale physical memory, the kernel must execute a TLB Shootdown: 1. The initiating core generates an Inter-Processor Interrupt (IPI) broadcast across the system interconnect to all sibling cores. 2. The sibling cores freeze execution, flush their local TLBs using the INVLPG instruction, and acknowledge the IPI. 3. The initiating core waits for all acknowledgments before proceeding.
On 128-core servers, high-frequency TLB shootdowns introduce massive synchronization overhead, consuming significant CPU cycles in interrupt handlers.

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
section: x86-64 Paging: Four-Level and Five-Level Page Tables
text:
x86-64 Paging: Four-Level and Five-Level Page Tables
In 64-bit mode, modern x86 processors implement two paging models:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        x86-64 4-LEVEL PAGE TRANSLATION                 │
│                                                                        │
│   Virtual Address (48 bits):                                           │
│   [47 ... 39]  [38 ... 30]  [29 ... 21]  [20 ... 12]  [11 ........ 0]  │
│     PGD (9b)     PUD (9b)     PMD (9b)     PTE (9b)     Offset (12b)   │
│        │            │            │            │               │        │
│   CR3 ─┘            │            │            │               │        │
│    │                │            │            │               │        │
│    ▼                ▼            ▼            ▼               ▼        │
│   [PGD Table] ──► [PUD Table] ─► [PMD Table] ─► [PTE Table] ──► + Offset│
│                                                               = PhysAddr│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. Four-Level Paging (4-Level / 48-bit Canonical Addressing)
Uses bits 0 to 47 of the virtual address, providing a \(256\text{ TiB}\) address space split evenly between user-space (\(128\text{ TiB}\)) and kernel-space (\(128\text{ TiB}\)). Bits 48 to 63 must be a sign-extension of bit 47 (canonical address rule): - Level 4: Page Global Directory (PGD) (9 bits \(\rightarrow\) 512 entries) - Level 3: Page Upper Directory (PUD) (9 bits \(\rightarrow\) 512 entries) - Level 2: Page Middle Directory (PMD) (9 bits \(\rightarrow\) 512 entries) - Level 1: Page Table Entry (PTE) (9 bits \(\rightarrow\) 512 entries) - Physical Offset: Bits 0–11 (\(4096\text{ bytes}\)).


2. Five-Level Paging (5-Level Paging / 57-bit Addressing)
To support multi-petabyte memory configurations on modern server processors (Ice Lake, Sapphire Rapids, EPYC Genoa), Intel and AMD introduced 5-Level Paging (CONFIG_X86_5LEVEL): - Adds a fifth level: Page 4th Directory (P4D). - Expands virtual addressing to 57 bits (\(128\text{ Petabytes}\)).

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
section: ARM64 and RISC-V Virtual Memory Systems
text:
ARM64 and RISC-V Virtual Memory Systems

ARM64 (AArch64): Uses the Translation Table Base Registers (TTBR0_EL1 and TTBR1_EL1). TTBR0 translates user-space virtual addresses (0x0000...), while TTBR1 translates kernel virtual addresses (0xFFFF...), eliminating the need to swap address tables during system calls. Supports \(4\text{ KiB}\), \(16\text{ KiB}\), and \(64\text{ KiB}\) page granules.
RISC-V: Standardizes virtual memory into formal translation modes configured via the satp register:

Sv39: 3-level page tables (39-bit virtual address, 512 GiB space).
Sv48: 4-level page tables (48-bit virtual address, 256 TiB space).
Sv57: 5-level page tables (57-bit virtual address, 128 PiB space).

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
section: Memory Types, Caching Attributes, and Access Permissions
text:
Memory Types, Caching Attributes, and Access Permissions
Every 64-bit Page Table Entry (PTE) contains control flags evaluated by the MMU on every access:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        64-BIT PTE FORMAT (x86-64)                      │
│                                                                        │
│   63   62 ... 52  51 .................................... 12  11 ... 0 │
│  ┌───┬──────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────┬────────┐ │
│  │NX │ Available│ Physical Frame Address (PFN 40-bits)      │ Flags  │ │
│  └───┴──────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────┴────────┘ │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

P (Present - Bit 0): 1 if page resides in physical RAM; 0 if swapped out or unallocated (triggers page fault).
R/W (Read/Write - Bit 1): 0 = read-only; 1 = read-write.
U/S (User/Supervisor - Bit 2): 0 = Ring 0 kernel privilege only; 1 = Ring 3 user-space accessible.
PWT / PCD / PAT: Memory caching attributes: Write-Through, Cache-Disable (for MMIO registers), Write-Combining (for video framebuffers).
A (Accessed - Bit 5): Set to 1 by hardware whenever the page is read or written; used by Linux LRU reclaim.
D (Dirty - Bit 6): Set to 1 by hardware whenever the page is written to; used to track dirty writeback.
NX (No-Execute - Bit 63): Prevents instruction execution from data pages.

title: Chapter 2: Hardware Foundations and Address Translation
section: Walking a Page Table by Hand: A Practical Example
text:
Walking a Page Table by Hand: A Practical Example
Let us trace a virtual address translation by hand on x86-64:
Suppose an application accesses Virtual Address: \[\text{VA} = \texttt{0x00007FFF5A241C80}\]

Convert to Binary and Extract Field Offsets:

0x00007FFF5A241C80 in binary: \[\underbrace{0000000000000000}_{\text{Sign extension}} \underbrace{011111111}_{\text{PGD}} \underbrace{111010010}_{\text{PUD}} \underbrace{010010001}_{\text{PMD}} \underbrace{000001100}_{\text{PTE}} \underbrace{110010000000}_{\text{Offset}}\]
PGD Index: 011111111_2 = 0x0FF = 255
PUD Index: 111010010_2 = 0x1D2 = 466
PMD Index: 010010001_2 = 0x091 = 145
PTE Index: 000001100_2 = 0x00C = 12
Page Offset: 110010000000_2 = 0xC80

Step-by-Step Hardware Walk:

The CPU reads control register CR3 to get the base physical address of the PGD table (0x100000).
Reads entry at index 255: PGD[255] yields pointer to PUD table (0x205000).
Reads entry at index 466: PUD[466] yields pointer to PMD table (0x341000).
Reads entry at index 145: PMD[145] yields pointer to PTE table (0x489000).
Reads entry at index 12: PTE[12] contains physical frame address: 0x892A000 (PFN: 0x892A).
The CPU combines the physical frame address with the page offset: \[\text{Physical Address} = \texttt{0x892A000} + \texttt{0xC80} = \mathbf{\texttt{0x892AC80}}\]


The hardware issues a bus cycle to read physical byte 0x892AC80 from DRAM and populates the TLB for subsequent reads.

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
text:
Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
While hardware translation mechanics operate in units of pages and physical frames, the Linux kernel organizes memory from an architectural perspective: dividing the 64-bit virtual address continuum into well-defined user-space segments and privileged kernel zones.
Within user space, an executing application requires code segments, global initialized data, uninitialized BSS buffers, a dynamically expanding heap, thread execution stacks, and memory-mapped file regions. In kernel space, the kernel maintains direct 1:1 physical memory mappings, dynamically allocated vmalloc pools, and fixmapped I/O windows.
This chapter details the virtual memory architecture of Linux: the process address space layout, kernel virtual memory zones, architecture-specific splits, ASLR randomization, the core data structures (mm_struct and vm_area_struct), system call primitives (mmap, brk, mremap), and a hands-on experiment inspecting live process memory maps via /proc/[pid]/maps.

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
section: The Process Address Space in Linux
text:
The Process Address Space in Linux
On modern 64-bit architectures, the full 64-bit address space (\(16\text{ Exabytes}\)) is divided into two symmetrical halves separated by a non-canonical gap:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        64-BIT VIRTUAL MEMORY MAP (x86-64)              │
│                                                                        │
│   0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│                      │ High Kernel Fixmaps & VSYSCALL               │  │
│   0xFFFF888000000000 │ Direct Physical Memory Map (page_offset_base)│  │
│                      │ (Maps all physical RAM 1:1 with kernel base) │  │
│   0xFFFF800000000000 ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│                      │                                              │  │
│                      │ NON-CANONICAL "HOLE"                         │  │
│                      │ (Addresses invalid in hardware; 16 Exabytes) │  │
│                      │                                              │  │
│   0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF ├──────────────────────────────────────────────┤  │
│                      │ User Stack (grows downward)                  │  │
│                      │ Memory Mappings (mmap, shared libraries)     │  │
│                      │ Heap (brk - grows upward)                    │  │
│                      │ BSS & Data Segments                          │  │
│   0x0000000000400000 │ Text Segment (Executable Code)               │  │
│   0x0000000000000000 └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

User Space (0x0000000000000000 to 0x00007FFFFFFFFFFF): The lower \(128\text{ TiB}\). Accessible by unprivileged processes executing in Ring 3.
The Non-Canonical Hole: In 48-bit addressing, addresses from 0x0000800000000000 to 0xFFFF7FFFFFFFFFFF are rejected by CPU hardware. Dereferencing an address inside this range triggers a General Protection Fault (#GP).
Kernel Space (0xFFFF800000000000 to 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF): The upper \(128\text{ TiB}\). Accessible only in Ring 0 supervisor mode. Protected by hardware page table supervisor bits (U/S = 0).

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
section: User-Space Layout: Code, Data, Heap, Stack, and Mapped Regions
text:
User-Space Layout: Code, Data, Heap, Stack, and Mapped Regions
A process’s user-space memory is partitioned into distinct logical memory segments:

Text Segment (.text): Contains compiled machine code instructions. Marked read-only and executable (R-X). Multiple running instances of the same binary share the identical physical text pages.
Data Segment (.data): Stores globally initialized variables (e.g., int global_var = 42;). Marked read-write, non-executable (RW-).
BSS Segment (.bss): Stores uninitialized global and static variables (Block Started by Symbol). Does not occupy disk space in the ELF binary; initialized to zeros on first write via demand paging.
Heap: Contiguous memory managed by brk() and sbrk(), growing upward toward higher addresses. Used by runtime allocators (malloc) for dynamic memory.
Memory Mapping Segment (mmap): Placed below the stack, growing downward. Accommodates dynamically loaded shared libraries (libc.so), memory-mapped files, and large anonymous allocations.
User Stack: Stores local function variables, saved frame pointers, and return addresses. Grows downward from the top of user space (0x7FFFFFFFFFFF).

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
section: Kernel Virtual Address Space and Direct Mapping
text:
Kernel Virtual Address Space and Direct Mapping
The upper \(128\text{ TiB}\) kernel address space contains specialized memory areas:

Direct Mapping (page_offset_base): A massive virtual window (beginning at 0xffff888000000000 on x86-64) that maps the entirety of physical system RAM 1:1. A physical address \(P\) corresponds to virtual address: \[V = P + \text{PAGE\_OFFSET}\] Allows the kernel to access any physical frame without modifying page tables.
vmalloc Pool (VMALLOC_START to VMALLOC_END): Used to allocate virtually contiguous memory buffers that may be physically non-contiguous.
vmemmap: An array of struct page headers representing every physical page frame in system memory.

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
section: The mm_struct and vma_struct: Core Data Structures

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
section: Memory Region Management with mmap, brk, and mremap
text:
Memory Region Management with mmap, brk, and mremap
User-space processes modify their virtual address space through three primary system calls:

brk(void *addr): Moves the top of the process heap (the program break). Increasing brk expands heap virtual memory; decreasing it frees memory back to the kernel.
mmap(void *addr, size_t length, int prot, int flags, int fd, off_t offset): Creates a new VMA.

Anonymous Mapping (MAP_ANONYMOUS): Allocates RAM backed by zero-filled pages rather than a file; standard mechanism for large heap allocations.
File-Backed Mapping: Maps a disk file directly into the process address space; reads and writes translate into page cache operations without explicit read() or write() syscalls.

mremap(void *old_address, size_t old_size, size_t new_size, int flags): Expands or shrinks an existing VMA, relocating it to a new virtual address if adjacent virtual space is occupied.

title: Chapter 3: Linux Address Spaces and the Virtual Memory Layout
section: Practical Experiment: Inspecting Your Process’s Memory Map
text:
Practical Experiment: Inspecting Your Process’s Memory Map
Every running process exposes its complete VMA table through the procfs pseudo-filesystem:
# Launch a background shell and inspect its memory map
cat /proc/$$/maps | head -n 15
00400000-00452000 r-xp 00000000 08:01 1234567    /usr/bin/bash        # Text
00651000-00652000 r--p 00051000 08:01 1234567    /usr/bin/bash        # Read-only Data
00652000-0065b000 rw-p 00052000 08:01 1234567    /usr/bin/bash        # Data / BSS
01a2f000-01c4e000 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0          [heap]               # Heap (brk)
7f8a1000-7f8b0000 r-xp 00000000 08:01 9876543    /lib64/libc.so.6     # Shared Lib
7ffd8a40-7ffd8a61 rw-p 00000000 00:00 0          [stack]              # User Stack
7ffd8a78-7ffd8a7c r-xp 00000000 00:00 0          [vdso]               # Kernel vDSO
Each row represents an active vm_area_struct: - 00400000-00452000: Virtual address range (vm_start - vm_end). - r-xp: Permissions (read, write, execute, private / copy-on-write). - 00000000: File offset. - 08:01 1234567: Storage device major:minor and inode number. - [heap] / [stack]: Descriptive label.

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
text:
Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
At the foundation of all memory allocations—whether servicing a user-space malloc(), a kernel SLUB object cache, or an NVMe Direct Memory Access (DMA) ring buffer—lies the physical page allocator.
In Linux, physical RAM is managed in units of page frames (typically \(4\text{ KiB}\)). The kernel subsystem responsible for allocating and freeing contiguous physical page frames is the Buddy Allocator.
This chapter explores physical memory management: the ubiquitous struct page descriptor, memory nodes and zones, the binary buddy allocation algorithm, allocation orders, GFP (Get Free Page) flags, fragmentation mitigation (migrate types), NUMA node policies, and an architectural walkthrough of the kernel source file mm/page_alloc.c.

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
section: Tracking Physical Pages: The page Struct and Memmap

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
text:
Memory Zones and Node Architecture
Physical memory is partitioned into a hierarchy: Nodes \(\rightarrow\) Zones \(\rightarrow\) Page Frames.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        PHYSICAL MEMORY HIERARCHY                       │
│                                                                        │
│   NUMA Node 0 (Socket 0 DRAM)          NUMA Node 1 (Socket 1 DRAM)     │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐     ┌────────────────────────────┐  │
│   │ ZONE_DMA    (First 16 MiB)   │     │ ZONE_NORMAL (All DRAM)     │  │
│   │ ZONE_DMA32  (16 MiB - 4 GiB) │     │ ZONE_MOVABLE               │  │
│   │ ZONE_NORMAL (4 GiB - 64 GiB) │     └────────────────────────────┘  │
│   │ ZONE_MOVABLE                 │                                     │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘                                     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

ZONE_DMA: The first \(16\text{ MiB}\) of physical RAM, reserved for legacy ISA devices that cannot address beyond 24 bits.
ZONE_DMA32: Memory between \(16\text{ MiB}\) and \(4\text{ GiB}\), accessible by 32-bit PCI devices limited to 32-bit DMA addresses.
ZONE_NORMAL: Standard directly addressable memory used for regular kernel and user allocations.
ZONE_MOVABLE: Memory containing only movable pages (page cache and anonymous memory), used for hot-plug memory removal and memory compaction without pinning.

Each zone is represented by a struct zone containing free page lists, page counters, and watermark thresholds (WMARK_MIN, WMARK_LOW, WMARK_HIGH).

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
section: The Buddy Allocator Algorithm and Implementation
text:
The Buddy Allocator Algorithm and Implementation
The Buddy Allocator is designed to satisfy two requirements: 1. Allocate contiguous chunks of physical pages in powers of two. 2. Rapidly coalesce adjacent free chunks (buddies) back into larger blocks when freed, preventing external fragmentation.

Allocation Orders (\(0\) to \(10\))
The allocator categorizes free blocks into Orders (\(0 \le \text{Order} \le 10\)):
\[\text{Block Size} = 2^{\text{Order}} \times 4096\text{ bytes}\]



Order
Page Count
Contiguous Memory Size




0
1 page
\(4\text{ KiB}\)


1
2 pages
\(8\text{ KiB}\)


2
4 pages
\(16\text{ KiB}\)


…
…
…


9
512 pages
\(2\text{ MiB}\) (Huge Page boundary)


10
1,024 pages
\(4\text{ MiB}\) (Maximum allocation unit)



┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        BUDDY SPLITTING AND MERGING                     │
│                                                                        │
│   Initial State: One Order 3 Block (8 Pages)                           │
│   [Page 0] [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 3] [Page 4] [Page 5] [Page 6] [Page 7]│
│                                                                        │
│   Request: Allocate Order 1 Block (2 Pages)                            │
│   1. Split Order 3 -> Two Order 2 Blocks ([0..3] and [4..7])           │
│   2. Split Order 2 [0..3] -> Two Order 1 Buddies ([0..1] and [2..3])   │
│   3. Allocate [0..1] to caller. Remaining buddies placed on free lists: │
│      - Order 1 List: [2..3]                                            │
│      - Order 2 List: [4..7]                                            │
│                                                                        │
│   Freeing: When [0..1] is freed, the kernel checks its buddy [2..3].   │
│   If [2..3] is free, they coalesce instantly into Order 2 [0..3],      │
│   which coalesces with buddy [4..7] back into Order 3 [0..7]!         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The physical buddy of a page block is calculated using a bitwise XOR: \[\text{Buddy PFN} = \text{Block PFN} \oplus (1 \ll \text{Order})\]

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
section: Allocation Paths: GFP Flags and Context Sensitivity
text:
Allocation Paths: GFP Flags and Context Sensitivity
Kernel code requests pages using alloc_pages(gfp_mask, order):
struct page *page = alloc_pages(GFP_KERNEL, 0);
The Get Free Page (GFP) flags instruct the allocator how aggressively it may behave to find memory:

GFP_KERNEL: Standard process-context allocation. The calling thread may sleep, wait for I/O, or trigger page reclaim if memory is low.
GFP_ATOMIC: High-priority allocation for interrupt handlers and atomic spinlock regions. Must never sleep. Draws from emergency watermark memory pools.
GFP_DMA32: Forces allocation from ZONE_DMA32.
__GFP_ZERO: Automatically fills the allocated pages with zeros before returning.
__GFP_NOWARN: Suppresses kernel warning stack traces if the allocation fails.

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
text:
Fragmentation Analysis and Mitigation Strategies
Over time, random allocations and deallocations scatter pinned pages across the buddy lists, preventing the formation of contiguous Order 9 (\(2\text{ MiB}\)) blocks required for Transparent Huge Pages.

Grouping by Mobility (migrate_types)
Linux combats fragmentation by dividing free lists within each zone into distinct mobility classes: 1. MIGRATE_UNMOVABLE: Kernel code, core data structures, and DMA buffers. Cannot be relocated in memory. 2. MIGRATE_RECLAIMABLE: File-backed page cache folios and slab caches that can be shrunk or dropped under memory pressure. 3. MIGRATE_MOVABLE: User-space anonymous memory and buffers. The kernel can relocate these pages to new physical frames simply by updating the owning process’s page table entries.
By clustering unmovable allocations into dedicated physical page blocks, Linux prevents a single unmovable 4 KiB kernel page from spoiling a contiguous 2 MiB huge page block.
# Inspect buddyinfo free page counts across orders on your system
cat /proc/buddyinfo

title: Chapter 4: Physical Memory Management and the Buddy Allocator
text:
Source Walkthrough: mm/page_alloc.c
The entry point for all physical page allocation is __alloc_pages() in mm/page_alloc.c:
__alloc_pages(gfp_mask, order, preferred_nid, nodemask)
  │
  ├─► 1. Fast Path: get_page_from_freelist()
  │      Scan preferred zone free lists above WMARK_LOW.
  │      If free block exists: rmqueue() removes block from buddy list.
  │      Returns page immediately! (Latency: ~50 ns)
  │
  └─► 2. Slow Path: __alloc_pages_slowpath()
         Watermark fell below threshold.
         ├─ Wake kswapd background reclaim daemon.
         ├─ If GFP_ATOMIC: draw from emergency reserve pools.
         ├─ Compact memory (kcompactd) to synthesize contiguous blocks.
         ├─ Direct Reclaim: caller thread flushes dirty pages to disk.
         └─ Final resort: invoke the Out-of-Memory (OOM) killer!

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
text:
Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
While the Buddy Allocator manages memory in coarse \(4\text{ KiB}\) page frames, the Linux kernel rarely allocates memory in page-sized chunks. Kernel subsystems continuously allocate tiny objects: a 256-byte struct inode, a 192-byte struct dentry, a 160-byte network packet buffer (sk_buff), or a 32-byte timer descriptor.
If the kernel allocated a full \(4\text{ KiB}\) page frame for every 64-byte data structure, over 98% of physical memory would be lost to internal fragmentation.
To solve this, Linux employs the Slab Allocator Family. This chapter explores the architecture of kernel object caching: the historical SLAB allocator, the modern SLUB allocator, the embedded SLOB allocator, lockless per-CPU caches, the kmalloc family, cache line alignment, false sharing, and how to write a custom kernel module with a dedicated slab cache.

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
text:
Why Kernel Needs Specialized Allocators
Kernel object allocation exhibits distinct characteristics:

Repetitive Lifecycles: The kernel allocates and deallocates identical data structures millions of times per second (e.g., creating and destroying task_struct on every fork/exit, or allocating sk_buff on every incoming Ethernet packet).
Expensive Initialization: Initializing complex kernel objects involves setting up linked list pointers, initializing mutexes, spinlocks, and atomic reference counters. Reinitializing memory from scratch on every allocation wastes CPU cycles.
Internal Fragmentation Prevention: Sub-page allocators carve a \(4\text{ KiB}\) page into hundreds of uniform slots, ensuring zero internal waste.
Cache Warmth and CPU Affinity: Reusing recently freed objects keeps hot data inside CPU L1/L2 caches, eliminating DRAM bus stalls.

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
section: The Slab Allocator Design and History
text:
The Slab Allocator Design and History
Invented by Jeff Bonwick at Sun Microsystems for Solaris and adopted by Linux in 2.2, the SLAB allocator introduced Object Caching:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        TRADITIONAL SLAB DESIGN                         │
│                                                                        │
│   kmem_cache ("inode_cache", size = 256 B)                             │
│   ├── slabs_full   (All objects allocated)                             │
│   ├── slabs_partial (Some objects free; allocations serviced here)     │
│   └── slabs_empty  (All objects free; candidates for page reclaim)     │
│                                                                        │
│   Physical Slab (Contiguous 4 KiB Page Frame):                         │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ [kmem_bufctl (queue)] [Object 0] [Object 1] ... [Object 15]  │     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The original SLAB allocator maintained complex on-page metadata queues (kmem_bufctl) and three double-linked lists (slabs_full, slabs_partial, slabs_empty). On large multi-core servers, lock contention across these shared lists degraded scalability.

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
text:
Slub: Simplification and Performance Improvements
Authored by Christoph Lameter, SLUB is the default allocator in all modern Linux distributions. SLUB radically simplified internal mechanics by eliminating external list queues:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        SLUB IN-OBJECT FREELIST                         │
│                                                                        │
│   Slab Page (struct page repurposed):                                  │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ Object 0: [payload]                                          │     │
│   │ Object 1 (Free): [freelist_ptr ──► 0x... (points to Obj 3)] │     │
│   │ Object 2: [payload]                                          │     │
│   │ Object 3 (Free): [freelist_ptr ──► NULL (last free object)]  │     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

In-Object Free Lists: Unallocated objects store the pointer to the next free object directly inside their own uninitialized payload memory, requiring zero external metadata.
struct page Metadata: SLUB repurposes unused fields in the page frame’s struct page (page->freelist, page->inuse, page->objects), tracking slab status without allocating separate control descriptors.

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
section: SLOB: Minimalist Allocation for Embedded Systems
text:
SLOB: Minimalist Allocation for Embedded Systems
Simple List of Blocks (SLOB) was engineered for tiny embedded microcontrollers with minimal RAM (e.g., 8–32 MiB): - Implements a first-fit singly linked list algorithm over page frames. - Low memory footprint, but suffers from poor multi-core scaling and fragmentation. - Deprecated and formally removed in Linux 6.4 in favor of SLUB.

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
section: Per-CPU Caches and Lockless Fast Paths
text:
Per-CPU Caches and Lockless Fast Paths
To achieve millions of allocations per second across 128 CPU cores without lock contention, SLUB maintains a Per-CPU Cache (struct kmem_cache_cpu):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        SLUB PER-CPU ALLOCATION PATH                    │
│                                                                        │
│   Core 0 executes kmem_cache_alloc():                                  │
│   1. Read this_cpu_ptr(s->cpu_slab)->freelist                          │
│   2. If freelist != NULL:                                              │
│      - Atomically advance freelist pointer (cmpxchg_double)            │
│      - Return object pointer immediately! (ZERO LOCKS ACQUIRED, ~5 ns) │
│                                                                        │
│   3. If freelist == NULL (Local CPU Slab Exhausted):                   │
│      - Slow Path: Acquire node spinlock                                │
│      - Fetch partial slab from NUMA node list                          │
│      - If node empty: allocate new physical page from Buddy Allocator  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
By decoupling normal allocations from global locks, SLUB delivers near-perfect linear scaling across multi-socket systems.

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
section: kmalloc, kcalloc, and the Kernel Allocation API

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
section: Cache Colocation, False Sharing, and NUMA Effects
text:
Cache Colocation, False Sharing, and NUMA Effects
Memory performance on multi-core processors depends heavily on CPU L1/L2 cache line alignment (\(64\text{ bytes}\) on x86-64 and ARM64):

False Sharing: Occurs when two independent variables accessed concurrently by different CPU cores reside on the same 64-byte cache line. When Core 0 writes Variable A, the hardware cache coherency protocol (MESI/MOESI) invalidates the entire cache line on Core 1, forcing Core 1 to stall while re-fetching Variable B from L3 cache or DRAM.
Slab Cache Alignment: Always align performance-critical structures to cache line boundaries using SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN:
struct kmem_cache *cache = kmem_cache_create("my_cache", sizeof(struct my_struct),
                                             0, SLAB_HWCACHE_ALIGN, NULL);

title: Chapter 5: Kernel Memory Allocators: Slab, Slub, and SLOB
section: Building a Custom Kernel Allocator Module

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
text:
Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
While the kernel relies on the Buddy Allocator and SLUB for internal allocations, user-space applications depend on runtime dynamic memory allocators executing in Ring 3. Every call to malloc(), calloc(), or C++ new resolves through runtime allocator libraries (such as glibc’s ptmalloc3, jemalloc, or Google’s tcmalloc).
Concurrently, within the kernel itself, subsystems periodically need large buffers (several megabytes in size) that must be virtually contiguous to the software, but do not need to be physically contiguous in DRAM. For this, the kernel provides vmalloc().
This chapter explores user-space memory allocation engines, the boundary between brk() and mmap(), kernel vmalloc() and ioremap() mappings, performance trade-offs across allocators, and practical tracing of allocation behavior using eBPF.

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
section: The malloc Contract and POSIX Requirements
text:
The malloc Contract and POSIX Requirements
The POSIX standard for malloc() imposes strict operational contracts:

Alignment: Must return a pointer suitably aligned for any built-in scalar type (\(16\text{ bytes}\) on 64-bit platforms).
Reentrancy and Thread Safety: In multi-threaded programs, concurrent calls from separate threads must succeed without deadlocking or memory corruption.
Overhead Bounds: Allocators must maintain low metadata overhead per allocation and resist both internal fragmentation (wasted space inside an allocated chunk) and external fragmentation (inability to allocate because free memory is split into tiny pieces).

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
section: glibc ptmalloc: Arenas, Bins, and Thread Safety
text:
glibc ptmalloc: Arenas, Bins, and Thread Safety
The GNU C Library (glibc) implements ptmalloc3 (derived from Doug Lea’s dlmalloc):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        GLIBC PTMALLOC ARCHITECTURE                     │
│                                                                        │
│   Multi-Threaded Arenas:                                               │
│   ├─ Main Arena (Uses heap / brk)                                      │
│   └─ Thread Arenas (Created dynamically; uses mmap; up to 8x CPU cores)│
│                                                                        │
│   Chunk Bins (Categorized by Size):                                    │
│   ├─ Fastbins: Singly-linked LIFO caches (16 to 80 bytes; lock-free)   │
│   ├─ Tcache (Thread Local Cache): Lockless per-thread bins (< 1032 B)  │
│   ├─ Unsorted Bin: Holding area for recently freed chunks              │
│   ├─ Small Bins: Exact-size circular FIFO lists (< 512 bytes)          │
│   └─ Large Bins: Binned size ranges with skip lists (> 512 bytes)      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Thread Local Caching (Tcache): Merged in glibc 2.26, Tcache provides per-thread arrays of singly linked lists for allocations under \(1032\text{ bytes}\). Servicing an allocation from Tcache requires zero mutex synchronization, dramatically speeding up multi-threaded performance.
Per-Thread Arenas: To eliminate global mutex lock contention, ptmalloc creates multiple arenas. When a thread contends for an arena lock, it allocates a dedicated arena (up to \(8 \times \text{number of CPU cores}\) on 64-bit systems).

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
text:
Alternative Allocators: jemalloc and tcmalloc
For multi-threaded, high-throughput servers (such as Redis, MySQL, and Kubernetes runtimes), glibc’s ptmalloc can suffer from memory fragmentation and high memory footprints due to arena proliferation.

jemalloc (Jason Evans’ Allocator):

Standard in FreeBSD, Facebook services, and Redis.
Divides allocations into Small, Large, and Huge classes.
Implements fine-grained arenas indexed by thread ID, aggressive slab purging via madvise(MADV_DONTNEED), and built-in heap profiling.

tcmalloc (Thread-Caching Malloc by Google):

Optimizes aggressively for small object thread caches.
Employs lock-free thread-local caches and a central page heap managing \(4\text{ KiB}\) spans.


# Preload jemalloc into an existing application to eliminate ptmalloc fragmentation
LD_PRELOAD=/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2 ./my_server_app

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
section: mmap vs brk: Strategies for Large and Small Allocations
text:
mmap vs brk: Strategies for Large and Small Allocations
Dynamic memory allocators draw memory from the Linux kernel using two distinct syscall paths:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        MMAP VS BRK DECISION BOUNDARY                   │
│                                                                        │
│   Small Allocation (< MMAP_THRESHOLD, default 128 KiB):                │
│   ├─ Uses brk() / sbrk() to grow the heap segment                      │
│   ├─ Low syscall overhead: 1 brk() call amortized across 1000s of small│
│   │  allocations                                                       │
│   └─ Caveat: Freeing a small chunk in the middle does not return RAM   │
│      to the kernel until the top of the heap is lowered.               │
│                                                                        │
│   Large Allocation (>= MMAP_THRESHOLD):                                │
│   ├─ Uses mmap(MAP_ANONYMOUS | MAP_PRIVATE)                            │
│   ├─ Allocates independent VMA aligned to 4 KiB page boundary          │
│   └─ Advantage: When free() is called, munmap() returns physical RAM   │
│      to the kernel immediately!                                        │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The threshold parameter (M_MMAP_THRESHOLD) dynamically self-tunes in glibc between 128 KiB and 32 MiB based on observed allocation patterns.

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
section: vmalloc and the Kernel’s Virtual Memory Allocator
text:
vmalloc and the Kernel’s Virtual Memory Allocator
In kernel space, kmalloc() requires physically contiguous pages from the Buddy Allocator. If system memory is fragmented, attempting to allocate an Order 8 (\(1\text{ MiB}\)) physically contiguous buffer will fail with -ENOMEM.
For large kernel buffers where physical contiguity is unnecessary (e.g., loading large kernel modules or allocating firewall filter tables), the kernel provides vmalloc():
void *ptr = vmalloc(16 * 1024 * 1024); /* Allocate 16 MiB */
if (!ptr) return -ENOMEM;
vfree(ptr);
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        VMALLOC TRANSLATION MAPPING                     │
│                                                                        │
│   Virtual Memory Space (Contiguous 16 MiB in VMALLOC_START region)     │
│   [Page 0] [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 3] ... [Page 4095]                  │
│      │        │        │        │                                      │
│      ▼        ▼        ▼        ▼                                      │
│   Physical DRAM (Completely scattered, non-contiguous page frames)     │
│   [PFN 0x12] ... [PFN 0x89] ... [PFN 0x04] ... [PFN 0xE2]              │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
vmalloc() allocates independent Order 0 (\(4\text{ KiB}\)) pages from the Buddy Allocator across physical memory and builds custom kernel page table entries mapping them into a contiguous virtual address range inside the VMALLOC zone. - Cost: Slower than kmalloc() because it must allocate and populate page tables; induces TLB overhead. - Restriction: Cannot be used in interrupt contexts (GFP_ATOMIC) because page table allocation may sleep.

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
section: vmap, ioremap, and Special Mapping Regions
text:
vmap, ioremap, and Special Mapping Regions

ioremap(resource_size_t offset, unsigned long size): Maps physical hardware MMIO addresses (e.g., PCIe registers on a network card) into the kernel’s virtual address space, configuring page caching bits to Uncacheable (PWT=1, PCD=1) so CPU write buffers do not delay register reads.
vmap(struct page **pages, unsigned int count): Takes an array of existing physical page descriptors and maps them into a contiguous virtual window.

title: Chapter 6: User-Space Memory Allocation and vmalloc
section: Practical Experiment: Tracing malloc Behavior with eBPF
text:
Practical Experiment: Tracing malloc Behavior with eBPF
Using modern eBPF tracing tools (from the BCC toolkit), we can inspect memory allocation sizes and stack traces across a running process in real time:
# Trace all allocations made by process PID 1234
sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/memleak -p 1234 --combined-only
Attaching to process 1234...
[15:20:01] Top 5 active allocations:
  16384 bytes in 4 allocations from:
    malloc+0x24 [libc.so.6]
    WorkerThread::Init()+0x4a [my_app]
    start_thread+0xd9 [libc.so.6]

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
text:
Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
When a Linux process allocates virtual memory, creates child processes, or memory-maps massive multi-gigabyte files, the operating system does not eagerly allocate physical DRAM frames or copy data blocks. Instead, Linux relies on Lazy Evaluation: deferring work until the exact instruction cycle where an address is accessed.
This fundamental optimization is powered by Demand Paging and Copy-on-Write (COW), driven by hardware page fault interrupts.
This chapter explores the page fault lifecycle: major vs minor faults, the role of backing files, Copy-on-Write mechanics during fork(), memory sharing semantics (MAP_SHARED vs MAP_PRIVATE), and an architectural walkthrough of the kernel’s fault handler in mm/memory.c.

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
section: The Lazy Loading Philosophy: Demand Paging
text:
The Lazy Loading Philosophy: Demand Paging
Consider an executable binary such as /usr/bin/python3 (\(4\text{ MiB}\) in size). When the user executes the command:

The kernel does not read 4 MiB of machine code from NVMe storage into physical RAM.
The kernel merely establishes virtual memory areas (vm_area_struct) covering the addresses and configures the process’s page tables with the Present bit cleared (P = 0).
When the CPU instruction pointer jumps to main(), the MMU encounters P = 0 and triggers an interrupt: a Page Fault.
The kernel reads only the single \(4\text{ KiB}\) page containing main() into RAM, sets P = 1, and resumes the CPU.

Pages containing code for rarely used Python modules (e.g., legacy math libraries or cleanup handlers) are never read from disk if the script never invokes them.

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
section: Page Fault Types and Handling Flow
text:
Page Fault Types and Handling Flow
Page faults are not errors; they are the primary mechanism by which virtual memory is dynamically constructed:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        PAGE FAULT DECISION ENGINE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   MMU detects Present Bit == 0 or Permission Violation                 │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Interrupt 14 (#PF) -> do_page_fault()                       │
│   Find VMA containing faulting address (via mm->mm_mt Maple Tree)      │
│          │                                                             │
│          ├─► Address NOT in any valid VMA ──► SIGSEGV (Invalid Pointer)│
│          │                                                             │
│          ├─► Write to Read-Only VMA       ──► SIGSEGV (Perm Denied)    │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Address IS in a valid VMA:                                  │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ Anonymous Memory (Heap/Stack/BSS)                            │     │
│   │ ├─ Allocate zeroed page from Buddy Allocator                 │     │
│   │ └─ Install PTE with RW permissions -> MINOR FAULT            │     │
│   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤     │
│   │ File-Backed Page (Code/Data)                                 │     │
│   │ ├─ Check Page Cache: Cached in RAM?                          │     │
│   │ │  ├─ YES: Map page into PTE -> MINOR FAULT                  │     │
│   │ │  └─ NO:  Issue Block I/O read to disk -> MAJOR FAULT       │     │
│   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤     │
│   │ Copy-on-Write (COW) Fault                                    │     │
│   │ └─ Allocate new private page, copy 4 KiB, set PTE to writable│     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
section: Major and Minor Faults: Performance Implications
text:
Major and Minor Faults: Performance Implications
Page faults are categorized by their I/O requirements:

Minor Page Fault: Resolved entirely in memory without accessing secondary storage. Examples: allocating a zero-filled heap page, resolving a COW write, or mapping a file page that is already cached in the kernel page cache.

Latency: \(1\text{ to } 5\text{ microseconds}\).

Major Page Fault: Requires reading data from physical disk (block device) or pulling a page back from swap storage. The faulting thread must sleep until the I/O completion interrupt fires.

Latency: \(50\text{ to } 500\text{ microseconds}\) (NVMe SSD) or \(5\text{ to } 15\text{ milliseconds}\) (spinning HDD).


# Observe major and minor fault rates across the system
sar -B 1 5
A sudden spike in major page faults is the universal indicator of memory thrashing, indicating that the working set of the system exceeds physical RAM.

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
text:
Copy-on-Write Semantics and Implementation
The Unix process creation model relies on fork(): duplicating the parent process to create an identical child.
If fork() eagerly duplicated every physical page owned by a \(64\text{ GiB}\) in-memory Redis database, process creation would stall for several seconds and consume an additional 64 GiB of RAM.
Instead, Linux uses Copy-on-Write (COW):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        COPY-ON-WRITE (COW) MECHANICS                   │
│                                                                        │
│   Step 1: fork() is called                                             │
│   ├─ Child receives duplicated page tables pointing to SAME phys frames│
│   ├─ All writable pages are marked READ-ONLY in BOTH page tables       │
│   └─ Inode page reference count incremented (_refcount = 2)           │
│                                                                        │
│   Step 2: Parent or Child attempts write (MOV [addr], 42)              │
│   ├─ MMU triggers Page Fault (#PF) due to Write on Read-Only page      │
│   ├─ Kernel page fault handler detects VMA allows writing (VM_WRITE)   │
│   ├─ Allocates a NEW physical page from the Buddy Allocator            │
│   ├─ Copies 4 KiB data from original page to new page                  │
│   ├─ Updates faulting process PTE to point to new page with R/W bit set│
│   └─ Original page reference count decremented (_refcount = 1)         │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
If the child process immediately calls execve() (e.g., launching a sub-command), zero data pages are ever copied!

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
section: Shared Memory Regions and mmap SHARED vs PRIVATE
text:
Shared Memory Regions and mmap SHARED vs PRIVATE
When mapping files or memory with mmap(): - MAP_PRIVATE: Changes are private to the calling process and enforced via Copy-on-Write. Modifications are never written back to the backing file on disk. - MAP_SHARED: Modifications are visible to all other processes mapping the same region and are flushed directly back to the physical file on disk by kernel writeback daemons.

title: Chapter 7: Demand Paging, Page Faults, and Copy-on-Write
section: Source Walkthrough: The Page Fault Handler in mm/memory.c

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
text:
Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
Accessing persistent storage is several orders of magnitude slower than accessing dynamic RAM: reading a \(4\text{ KiB}\) block from system DRAM takes approximately \(50\text{ to } 80\text{ nanoseconds}\), while reading the identical block from a PCIe Gen4 NVMe solid-state drive takes \(10\text{ to } 50\text{ microseconds}\)—a latency disparity of nearly 1,000 to 1.
To bridge this vast performance chasm, the Linux kernel routes all filesystem read and write operations through a unified, in-RAM caching layer: the Page Cache.
This chapter details the page cache architecture: why caching transforms system throughput, the modern XArray data structure, page state machines, sequential readahead algorithms, dirty page writeback daemons, the historical evolution from buffer heads to extents and folios, and an experiment to measure live page cache hit rates.

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
section: Why Caching File Data in RAM Transforms Performance
text:
Why Caching File Data in RAM Transforms Performance
In traditional Unix systems, disk caching was divided into two disparate pools: 1. The Buffer Cache: Cached raw physical disk blocks from block devices. 2. The Page Cache: Cached virtual memory pages for memory-mapped files.
This dual-cache architecture wasted physical memory: reading a file via read() and simultaneously mapping it via mmap() resulted in duplicate copies of the same file data in RAM, requiring complex synchronization locks.
In Linux 2.4, the kernel unified these architectures into a single Unified Page Cache. Today: - All disk reads populate the page cache. - All standard buffered writes modify page cache pages in RAM. - Virtual memory mappings and filesystem read/write calls operate on the identical physical memory frames.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        UNIFIED PAGE CACHE FLOW                         │
│                                                                        │
│   read(fd, buf, 4096)                 mmap(..., PROT_READ, fd, 0)      │
│          │                                        │                    │
│          ▼                                        ▼                    │
│   VFS vfs_read()                       Process Page Table PTE          │
│          │                                        │                    │
│          └──────────────────┬─────────────────────┘                    │
│                             ▼                                          │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ Unified Page Cache (struct address_space)                    │     │
│   │ Key: (struct inode *, page_offset)                           │     │
│   │ Physical DRAM Page Frame                                     │     │
│   └─────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│                             ▼ Only on Cache Miss                       │
│   Block I/O Layer (BIO) ──► NVMe / SATA Controller ──► Storage Disk    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
section: Page Cache Data Structures: Radix Trees and XArrays
text:
Page Cache Data Structures: Radix Trees and XArrays
Every file in the filesystem is represented by an address_space structure (inode->i_mapping). To find whether page offset \(N\) of a file is currently cached in RAM, the kernel needs an ultra-fast associative lookup data structure.

From Radix Trees to XArrays
Historically, Linux organized page cache pages in a Radix Tree. In Linux 4.20+, Matthew Wilcox introduced the XArray (eXtensible Array):
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        XARRAY LOOKUP HIERARCHY                         │
│                                                                        │
│   File Offset Index: 0x0004A12B (32-bit chunk index)                   │
│   [Bits 31..18]        [Bits 17..12]        [Bits 11..6]    [Bits 5..0]│
│   Root Chunk           Level 2              Level 1         Leaf Slot  │
│       │                    │                    │               │      │
│       ▼                    ▼                    ▼               ▼      │
│   [xa_node 64-way] ──► [xa_node 64-way] ──► [xa_node] ──► struct folio*│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

64-Way Radix Branches: Each xa_node contains 64 pointers, indexed by 6-bit slices of the file offset.
Lockless RCU Traversal: XArray lookups operate under Read-Copy Update (RCU). Thousands of concurrent reader threads can look up cached pages in the XArray simultaneously without acquiring locks or causing CPU cache-line bouncing.
Modern Compound Folios: In modern kernels, the XArray stores pointers to struct folio, representing variable-sized multi-page chunks (\(4\text{ KiB}\) to \(2\text{ MiB}\)) rather than individual pages.

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
section: Page State Machine and Lifecycle Management
text:
Page State Machine and Lifecycle Management
A page inside the page cache transitions through well-defined states tracked by atomic flags in page->flags:

Allocated: An empty physical page frame is allocated from the Buddy Allocator and inserted into the file’s XArray. Marked with PG_locked.
Reading: The kernel submits an asynchronous Block I/O read (bio) to the storage drive.
Uptodate (PG_uptodate): The DMA transfer completes; the page contains valid, synchronized file data. The lock is released.
Referenced & Active (PG_referenced, PG_active): Process reads the page; page is promoted on the LRU lists.
Dirty (PG_dirty): An application calls write(), modifying bytes in RAM. The page is now out of sync with disk storage.
Writeback (PG_writeback): The background flusher begins transferring the page to physical disk.
Clean: Disk write completes; PG_dirty and PG_writeback are cleared. The page can now be reclaimed immediately if memory is needed.

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
text:
Readahead Algorithms and Prefetching Strategies
When an application reads a file sequentially, waiting for disk I/O on every consecutive \(4\text{ KiB}\) page destroys throughput.
ext4 and the page cache implement Dynamic Asynchronous Readahead: - Initial Read: When a process reads the first \(4\text{ KiB}\), the kernel speculatively issues an I/O request for the next 16 to 32 pages (\(64\text{ KiB}\) to \(128\text{ KiB}\)). - Window Scaling: As the application continues sequential reads, the kernel dynamically doubles the readahead window up to \(512\text{ KiB}\) or \(2\text{ MiB}\). - Background I/O: The prefetch I/O runs asynchronously in the background. By the time the user application reaches block 30, the data has already arrived in RAM, transforming disk reads into zero-latency memory copies.

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
section: Dirty Pages, Writeback, and Flush Daemons
text:
Dirty Pages, Writeback, and Flush Daemons
Buffered writes are committed to persistent disk storage asynchronously by dedicated kernel background threads: kworker/flush (formerly pdflush and bdi-default-flush).

The Writeback Triggers

Periodic Timer: Every 5 seconds (configurable via vm.dirty_writeback_centisecs), flush threads wake up and write back pages that have been dirty longer than 30 seconds (vm.dirty_expire_centisecs).
Background Memory Ratio: When dirty memory exceeds vm.dirty_background_ratio (e.g., 10% of total RAM), flusher threads start background I/O to drain dirty pages.
Hard Throttle Ratio: If dirty memory reaches vm.dirty_ratio (e.g., 20% of total RAM), any process issuing write() is throttled: the process is forced to sleep and execute synchronous writeback itself before returning to user space.
Explicit Sync: System calls fsync(), fdatasync(), or sync() force immediate, synchronous flushing.

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
section: Buffer Heads, Extents, and Historical Evolution
text:
Buffer Heads, Extents, and Historical Evolution
In early Linux, every \(4\text{ KiB}\) page frame was associated with four 1 KiB Buffer Heads (struct buffer_head) to track individual physical disk sectors.
On high-throughput modern SSDs, maintaining buffer head descriptors introduces severe memory overhead and CPU spinlock contention. Modern filesystems (ext4 with extents, XFS, Btrfs) bypass buffer heads for data pages, submitting direct multi-page Block I/O requests (bio) mapped directly from extent ranges. Buffer heads are retained only for legacy metadata tracking.

title: Chapter 8: The Page Cache and Buffer Head Architecture
section: Practical Experiment: Measuring Page Cache Hit Rates
text:
Practical Experiment: Measuring Page Cache Hit Rates
Using the cachestat eBPF tool from BCC, we can observe the live hit rate of the Linux page cache across all running processes:
# Monitor page cache hits, misses, and dirties every 2 seconds
sudo /usr/share/bcc/tools/cachestat 2
   HITS   MISSES  DIRTIES    HITRATIO   BUFFERS_MB  CACHED_MB
 142051       42      102      99.97%          214      12480
 189402       12      310      99.99%          214      12482
  45210    12401     1205      78.47%          214      12530
A hit ratio drop below 90% indicates that the active workload working set exceeds available RAM, forcing frequent physical storage reads.
