title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
text:
Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
No matter how many gigabytes or terabytes of physical DRAM are provisioned on a server, memory consumption will eventually approach capacity. When available memory falls below kernel watermark thresholds, the operating system faces a critical architectural decision: Which physical pages should be evicted or swapped, and when?
A flawed eviction policy evicts hot pages, throwing the system into severe disk thrashing where the CPU spends 99% of its cycles waiting for swapped-out memory to reload. A robust policy smoothly balances file cache shrinking with anonymous page swapping, maintaining high system throughput.
This chapter details the Linux reclaim architecture: dual active/inactive LRU lists, page replacement heuristics, swap space mechanics, compressed in-RAM caching (zswap), thrashing prevention, and practical tuning of vm.swappiness.

title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
section: When RAM Runs Out: The Reclaim Problem
text:
When RAM Runs Out: The Reclaim Problem
Physical memory pages belong to two distinct categories:

File-Backed Pages (Page Cache): Pages backed by files on disk (executables, shared libraries, data files).

Clean Page: Can be discarded instantly with zero I/O; if needed later, the kernel re-reads the data from the backing file.
Dirty Page: Must be flushed to disk before the physical page frame can be reclaimed.

Anonymous Pages: Pages that have no backing file on disk (heap memory, stack variables, BSS segments, anonymous mmap allocations).

Cannot be discarded! The data must either be preserved in physical RAM or written to dedicated secondary backing storage: the Swap Space.

title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
text:
Active and Inactive Page Lists
To determine which pages are cold candidates for eviction, Linux maintains dual linked lists per memory zone:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        DUAL LRU LIST ARCHITECTURE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   New Allocation ──► Enters INACTIVE List (Head)                       │
│                             │                                          │
│                             ▼ Accessed again? (Hardware Referenced Bit)│
│                      ┌──────┴──────┐                                   │
│                      ▼ YES         ▼ NO (Remains unreferenced)         │
│   Promote to ACTIVE List           Migrate toward Inactive List Tail   │
│   (Hot working set pages)          (Cold pages targeted for reclaim)   │
│          │                                 │                           │
│          ▼ Aging pass                      ▼                           │
│   Demote cold pages back ──────────► Reclaim / Swap Out                │
│   to Inactive List                                                     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The kernel tracks four distinct lists per NUMA node: - anon_inactive: Cold anonymous pages eligible for swapping. - anon_active: Hot anonymous pages actively accessed by processes. - file_inactive: Cold file cache pages eligible for clean dropping. - file_active: Hot file cache pages actively referenced.

The Clock-Pro / Pseudo-LRU Heuristic
Linux does not maintain a perfect Least Recently Used (LRU) list because moving a page to the front of a linked list on every single memory access would cause severe lock contention across CPU cores.
Instead, Linux uses a Two-Hand Clock Heuristic: - When the hardware MMU translates an address, it sets the page’s hardware Accessed Bit (A = 1). - The kernel’s reclaim scanner periodically clears the bit (A = 0). - If the bit remains 0 on the subsequent scanner pass, the page has not been touched and is demoted to the inactive list for eviction.

title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
section: Swap Spaces, Swap Devices, and File-Based Swapping
text:
Swap Spaces, Swap Devices, and File-Based Swapping
Swap storage can be provisioned as a dedicated raw block partition (/dev/nvme0n1p3) or as a dynamic swap file on an existing filesystem (/swapfile):
# Create and activate a 4 GiB swap file
sudo fallocate -l 4G /swapfile
sudo chmod 0600 /swapfile
sudo mkswap /swapfile
sudo swapon /swapfile

The Swap Map and Swap Slots
Inside the kernel, swap space is divided into \(4\text{ KiB}\) Swap Slots. When an anonymous page is selected for swapping: 1. A free swap slot is allocated from the swap device. 2. The page data is written to the swap slot via Block I/O. 3. The process’s Page Table Entry (PTE) is updated: the Present bit is cleared (P = 0), and the physical frame address is replaced with a Swap Identifier (device index + slot offset). 4. The physical DRAM page frame is freed back to the Buddy Allocator.
When the process subsequently attempts to read the swapped-out address, the MMU triggers a page fault. The kernel reads the swap slot identifier from the PTE, reads the data block back from disk into a fresh DRAM frame (Swap-In), sets P = 1, and frees the swap slot.

title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
text:
zswap, z3fold, and Compressed Caching
Writing anonymous pages to persistent NVMe or SATA storage incurs high I/O latency. To eliminate this bottleneck, Linux includes zswap: a compressed, in-RAM write-behind cache for swap pages.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        ZSWAP COMPRESSION PIPELINE                      │
│                                                                        │
│   Page Eviction selected for Swap-Out                                  │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Intercepted by zswap                                        │
│   Compress 4 KiB Page using LZ4 / ZSTD (Latency: ~2 microseconds)      │
│          │                                                             │
│          ▼ Achieved 3:1 Compression Ratio?                             │
│   ┌──────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ YES: Store compressed 1.3 KiB payload in zpool (z3fold/zsmalloc)│  │
│   │      Avoids physical disk I/O completely! (100x faster swap-in) │  │
│   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤     │
│   │ NO:  Pass uncompressed page through to physical swap disk    │     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Compression Algorithms: Typically configured to use LZ4 (fastest) or Zstandard (ZSTD) (highest compression ratio).
Memory Pool Allocators (zsmalloc / z3fold): Packs multiple compressed page fragments into single physical page frames, eliminating internal fragmentation.

# Verify zswap status and compression ratio
grep -r . /sys/kernel/debug/zswap/

title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
text:
Thrashing Detection and Prevention
When active process memory significantly exceeds physical RAM, the kernel enters Thrashing: pages swapped out are immediately referenced and swapped back in, while file cache is completely purged.

Pressure Stall Information (PSI)
Modern Linux kernels monitor memory health via PSI (Pressure Stall Information) in /proc/pressure/memory:
cat /proc/pressure/memory
# some avg10=2.40 avg60=1.10 avg300=0.45 total=1240189
# full avg10=0.80 avg60=0.30 avg300=0.10 total=482101

some: Percentage of time that at least one CPU task was stalled waiting for memory reclaim or swap I/O.
full: Percentage of time that all non-idle tasks were completely blocked waiting for memory (catastrophic thrashing). Production orchestrators (systemd-oomd, Kubernetes) monitor PSI to shed load before complete system lockups.

title: Chapter 9: Swapping, Reclaim, and Page Replacement Policies
section: Practical Experiment: Tuning vm.swappiness and Observing Behavior
text:
Practical Experiment: Tuning vm.swappiness and Observing Behavior
The kernel parameter vm.swappiness (ranging from 0 to 200, default 60) controls the relative ratio of reclaiming anonymous memory vs reclaiming file-backed page cache:
\[\text{Swap Tendency} = \frac{\text{swappiness} \times \text{Anon Inactive Ratio}}{100}\]
# Query current swappiness
sysctl vm.swappiness

# Server Tuning: Reduce swapping aggressiveness to prioritize keeping anon memory in RAM
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=10

# Desktop / Container Host Tuning: Aggressive swapping to preserve large file caches
sudo sysctl -w vm.swappiness=100

swappiness = 0: The kernel will never initiate swap until available memory falls below the absolute emergency zone watermarks.
swappiness = 100: The kernel treats anonymous memory and file page cache with equal eviction weight.
swappiness = 200: The kernel aggressively swaps out idle anonymous memory to preserve maximum file cache capacity.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
text:
Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
In modern computing, translation overhead is a significant bottleneck. With standard \(4\text{ KiB}\) pages, a database server with 256 GiB of RAM requires \(67\text{ million}\) distinct page table entries. The CPU’s on-chip Translation Lookaside Buffer (TLB)—holding only a few thousand entries—suffers continuous TLB misses, spending up to 20–30% of execution cycles stalling on hardware page table walks.
To maximize TLB reach, modern processors and Linux support Huge Pages: mapping memory in chunks of \(2\text{ MiB}\) (Order 9) or \(1\text{ GiB}\) (Order 18).
However, allocating a 2 MiB huge page requires finding 512 physically contiguous \(4\text{ KiB}\) page frames. In long-running servers, memory fragmentation scatters allocations, breaking up contiguous chunks.
This chapter explores how Linux solves this dual challenge: memory compaction algorithms, kcompactd daemons, Transparent Huge Pages (THP), static hugetlbfs pools, and measuring the performance impact of huge pages.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
text:
Fragmentation in Long-Running Systems
External memory fragmentation occurs when total free memory is abundant, but no single contiguous chunk of physical frames is large enough to satisfy a high-order allocation request:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        PHYSICAL FRAGMENTATION DILEMMA                  │
│                                                                        │
│   Zone Memory (32 KiB total free space):                               │
│   [4K Free] [4K Pinned] [4K Free] [4K Pinned] [4K Free] [4K Free]      │
│                                                                        │
│   Request: Allocate Order 2 Block (16 KiB contiguous):                │
│   - Total Free RAM = 16 KiB                                            │
│   - BUT maximum contiguous span is only 8 KiB!                         │
│   - Result: ALLOCATION FAILS unless memory is compacted!               │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
section: The Compaction Algorithm: Migration and Scanning
text:
The Compaction Algorithm: Migration and Scanning
To restore contiguous blocks without evicting data to disk, Linux employs Memory Compaction:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        TWO-POINTER COMPACTION SCAN                     │
│                                                                        │
│   Zone Start                                                  Zone End │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ [Used] [Free] [Used] [Used] ...... [Free] [Used] [Free] [Used│     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
│       ▲                                                ▲               │
│       │                                                │               │
│   Migration Scanner (moves right)              Free Scanner (moves left│
│   Finds movable pages to relocate              Finds free target slots │
│                                                                        │
│   Action: Move allocated page from start into free slot at end.        │
│   Result: Coalesces contiguous free pages at the start of the zone!    │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The algorithm operates via two converging pointers within each memory zone: 1. Migration Scanner: Starts at the beginning of the zone, scanning forward to identify allocated, movable anonymous or page cache pages. 2. Free Scanner: Starts at the end of the zone, scanning backward to identify empty, unallocated page slots. 3. Page Relocation: The kernel copies page data from the migration scanner’s location to the free scanner’s slot, updates the process’s page table entries to point to the new physical frame address, and flushes local TLBs. 4. Coalescence: The vacated slots coalesce under the Buddy Allocator, synthesizing clean high-order blocks.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
section: Direct Reclaim vs kswapd vs Compact Daemons
text:
Direct Reclaim vs kswapd vs Compact Daemons
Compaction is executed in three operational modes:

Background Compaction (kcompactd): Autonomous kernel threads wake up when the number of high-order free blocks falls below the zone low watermark, performing proactive, low-overhead compaction in the background.
Direct Compaction: If an allocation request with __GFP_DIRECT_RECLAIM fails and background compaction has not caught up, the calling thread is paused and forced to run the compaction scanner synchronously.
Proactive Compaction (vm.compaction_proactiveness): Introduced in Linux 5.8, periodically scans and defragments memory during idle CPU windows to maintain a high baseline of contiguous blocks.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
text:
Huge Pages and TLB Efficiency
A single TLB entry for a standard page covers \(4\text{ KiB}\). A single TLB entry for a Huge Page covers:
\[2\text{ MiB} = 2,097,152\text{ bytes} \quad (512 \times \text{larger TLB coverage!})\]
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        TLB REACH COMPARISON (1024 ENTRIES)             │
│                                                                        │
│   Standard 4 KiB Pages:  1024 entries x 4 KiB   = 4 MiB TLB Reach      │
│   Huge 2 MiB Pages:      1024 entries x 2 MiB   = 2 GiB TLB Reach      │
│   Giant 1 GiB Pages:     1024 entries x 1 GiB   = 1 TiB TLB Reach      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
For workloads with massive active working sets (in-memory analytics, PostgreSQL, JVM applications), huge pages reduce TLB misses from millions per second to near zero, boosting instructions per cycle (IPC) by 15–30%.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
section: Transparent Huge Pages: Automatic Promotion and Demotion
text:
Transparent Huge Pages: Automatic Promotion and Demotion
Traditional huge pages required modifying application source code to invoke special APIs. Transparent Huge Pages (THP) automates this entirely within the kernel:

Transparent Allocation: When an application allocates a large anonymous buffer via mmap() or malloc(), the kernel speculatively backs the allocation with a single \(2\text{ MiB}\) compound physical page mapped directly at the Page Middle Directory (PMD) level.
Khugepaged Background Promotion: The khugepaged daemon continuously scans process memory. If it discovers 512 contiguous \(4\text{ KiB}\) pages that can be unified, it allocates a 2 MiB huge page, copies the data, updates the PMD entry to point to the huge page, and frees the 512 small pages.
Page Splitting: If an application subsequently calls munmap() or mprotect() on a 4 KiB slice of a huge page, the kernel transparently splits the 2 MiB compound page back into 512 individual 4 KiB page entries.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
section: hugetlbfs and Preallocated Huge Page Pools
text:
hugetlbfs and Preallocated Huge Page Pools
While THP is transparent, it cannot guarantee availability: if memory is heavily fragmented, the kernel falls back to standard 4 KiB pages.
For mission-critical workloads (e.g., KVM hypervisors, DPDK packet processing, Oracle databases), administrators allocate dedicated, non-swappable huge page pools at boot using hugetlbfs:
# Preallocate 2048 x 2 MiB huge pages (4 GiB total)
sudo sysctl -w vm.nr_hugepages=2048

# Mount hugetlbfs filesystem
sudo mount -t hugetlbfs none /dev/hugepages
Applications open files under /dev/hugepages or pass MAP_HUGETLB to mmap(), guaranteeing 100% huge page backing without fallback.

title: Chapter 10: Memory Compaction, Defragmentation, and Huge Pages
section: Practical Experiment: Enabling and Measuring THP Effects
text:
Practical Experiment: Enabling and Measuring THP Effects
THP modes are configured via /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled:
# Modes: [always] madvise never
# 'always': Automatically back all eligible memory with THP
# 'madvise': Back with THP only if application requests it via madvise(..., MADV_HUGEPAGE)
echo madvise | sudo tee /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled

# Measure active THP usage across the system
grep -i AnonHugePages /proc/meminfo

title: Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
text:
Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
In early symmetric multiprocessing (SMP) systems, all CPU cores connected to physical RAM through a single, shared system bus. As server architectures scaled to dozens and hundreds of CPU cores, the shared memory bus became an insurmountable bottleneck: cores spent the majority of their time stalled, arbitrating for bus access.
Modern multi-socket enterprise servers solve this by adopting Non-Uniform Memory Access (NUMA). In NUMA architectures, physical memory is partitioned: each CPU socket owns a local memory controller and local DRAM channels, connecting to adjacent sockets across high-speed point-to-point coherent interconnects (AMD Infinity Fabric, Intel Ultra Path Interconnect - UPI).
While NUMA provides immense total memory bandwidth, access times are non-uniform: reading local memory takes \(60\text{ to } 80\text{ ns}\), while reading remote memory across an interconnect link takes \(120\text{ to } 160\text{ ns}\)—a 2x latency penalty accompanied by interconnect bus saturation.
This chapter explores how Linux manages NUMA topologies: the pg_data_t node hierarchy, NUMA memory allocation policies, automatic NUMA balancing, task placement coordination, and NUMA-aware systems programming.

title: Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
text:
The NUMA Problem: Distance Matters
In a dual-socket server with 64 cores per socket:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        DUAL-SOCKET NUMA TOPOLOGY                       │
│                                                                        │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐    Interconnect    ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │
│   │ Socket 0 (NUMA Node 0)       │◄── (UPI/Infinity) ─►│ Socket 1 (NUMA Node 1)       │ │
│   │ Cores 0-63                   │                    │ Cores 64-127                 │ │
│   │ Local Memory Controller      │                    │ Local Memory Controller      │ │
│   └──────────────┬───────────────┘                    └──────────────┬───────────────┘ │
│                  │ (Local DRAM: ~70 ns)                              │ (Local DRAM: ~70 ns)
│                  ▼                                                   ▼                 │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────┐                    ┌──────────────────────────────┐ │
│   │ Local DRAM (256 GiB)         │                    │ Local DRAM (256 GiB)         │ │
│   └──────────────────────────────┘                    └──────────────────────────────┘ │
│                  ▲                                                   ▲                 │
│                  └────────── Remote Read (~140 ns) ──────────────────┘                 │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
The performance impact is governed by the NUMA Distance Ratio: - Local Memory Access: Distance \(10\) (Baseline latency). - Remote Socket Access: Distance \(20\) to \(32\) (\(2\times \text{ to } 3.2\times \text{ higher latency}\)).
If an application thread running on Core 0 on Socket 0 allocates memory that is placed in Node 1’s DRAM, every memory access must traverse the physical inter-socket interconnect. If dozens of threads do this concurrently, the interconnect links saturate, degrading application throughput by up to 50%.

title: Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
section: Node, Zone, and Memory Hierarchy in Linux

title: Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
section: Memory Policies: Default, Interleave, Bind, and Prefer
text:
Memory Policies: Default, Interleave, Bind, and Prefer
Linux provides fine-grained control over NUMA allocation policies via set_mempolicy(2) and the numactl command:

MPOL_DEFAULT: Memory is allocated on the local node where the allocating CPU core is currently executing.
MPOL_BIND: Memory must strictly be allocated from a specified set of nodes. If those nodes run out of memory, the allocation fails (-ENOMEM) rather than spilling over to other nodes. Essential for latency-critical database instances pinned to specific cores.
MPOL_INTERLEAVE: Memory allocations round-robin page-by-page across multiple nodes (\(4\text{ KiB}\) on Node 0, \(4\text{ KiB}\) on Node 1). Ideal for shared read-heavy caches accessed equally by threads on both sockets, distributing bandwidth across memory controllers.
MPOL_PREFERRED: Strongly prefers a specific node, but permits falling back to remote nodes if the preferred node is exhausted.

# Pin an application to execute only on Socket 0 cores using Socket 0 memory
numactl --cpunodebind=0 --membind=0 ./high_performance_db

# Interleave memory across all available NUMA nodes
numactl --interleave=all ./shared_cache_service

title: Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
section: Task Migration and Memory Placement Coordination
text:
Task Migration and Memory Placement Coordination
A common failure mode in multi-socket systems is Thread Migration: 1. A thread starts executing on Socket 0 and allocates 30 GiB of local memory in Node 0. 2. The Linux CFS/EEVDF CPU scheduler detects that Socket 1 is idle and migrates the thread to Socket 1. 3. Suddenly, 100% of the thread’s memory accesses become expensive remote accesses across the interconnect link!

Automatic NUMA Balancing (kernel.numa_balancing)
To correct this, modern Linux kernels include Auto-NUMA Balancing: - The kernel periodically marks a subset of the process’s page table entries as inaccessible (PROT_NONE). - When the thread accesses the page, a soft NUMA Hinting Page Fault triggers. - The fault handler inspects the CPU core executing the fault: - If the thread is executing on Socket 1, but the page resides on Node 0, the kernel tracks migration hints. - If access frequency remains high, the kernel either migrates the page across the bus to Node 1’s DRAM, or signals the CPU scheduler to migrate the thread back to Socket 0.

title: Chapter 11: NUMA, Memory Policy, and Scalability
text:
Performance Measurement and NUMA-Aware Programming
Inspect NUMA topology and memory allocation distribution:
# Display hardware NUMA node distances and core mapping
numactl --hardware

# View real-time per-node memory allocation statistics
numastat -m
Per-node memory (MB):
                          Node 0          Node 1           Total
                 --------------- --------------- ---------------
Active                   24102.4         18201.1         42303.5
Inactive                 12091.2         14012.8         26104.0
MemFree                   8102.5         14201.9         22304.4
Node Distances:
node   0   1 
  0:  10  21 
  1:  21  10 
numastat tracks two vital counters: - numa_hit: Successful allocations from the local NUMA node. - numa_miss: Allocations intended for local node that spilled to remote node due to low memory. High numa_miss indicates severe local memory imbalance.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
text:
Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
In modern cloud-native architectures, physical servers rarely execute a single monolithic application. Instead, hosts run dozens of containerized microservices (Docker, containerd, Kubernetes pods) collocated on a shared Linux kernel.
If an unprivileged container experiences a memory leak, it could consume all available physical memory on the host, triggering the host-level Out-of-Memory (OOM) killer to terminate critical system services (such as sshd, kubelet, or adjacent database instances).
To provide multi-tenant isolation, Linux utilizes Control Groups (cgroups) and the dedicated Memory Controller (memcg).
This chapter explores memory cgroups: the cgroups v2 hierarchy, memory accounting models, high vs max limit thresholds, hierarchical reclaim pressure, swap isolation, container OOM semantics, and a hands-on experiment configuring memory-limited cgroups.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
section: Containerization and the Need for Memory Isolation
text:
Containerization and the Need for Memory Isolation
Containers are not virtual machines; they do not have independent kernels or private DRAM allocations. Every process inside a container calls the identical kernel memory allocation routines (do_page_fault, alloc_pages, kmem_cache_alloc).
Without resource constraints, a container has an unrestricted view of the host’s physical RAM: - A Java Virtual Machine (JVM) inside a container on a 128 GiB host will calculate its default heap size as \(32\text{ GiB}\) (\(25\%\) of host RAM), even if the container was intended to run with only 512 MiB! - A process allocating memory in a loop will exhaust host memory, causing “noisy neighbor” failures across unrelated workloads.
The Memory Cgroup Controller acts as a virtual boundary, enforcing strict accounting, reclaim, and containment on subsets of processes.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
section: Cgroup Hierarchy and Memory Controller Architecture
text:
Cgroup Hierarchy and Memory Controller Architecture
In cgroups v2 (standard in modern Linux distributions), all resource controllers are organized into a single, unified tree mounted at /sys/fs/cgroup/:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        CGROUPS V2 UNIFIED MEMORY TREE                  │
│                                                                        │
│   /sys/fs/cgroup/ (Root Cgroup - Unlimited)                            │
│   ├── system.slice/ (System daemons: sshd, systemd-journald)           │
│   │   └─ memory.min = 2G (Protected memory; immune to reclaim)        │
│   │                                                                    │
│   └── kubepods.slice/ (Container workloads)                            │
│       ├── pod_frontend/                                                │
│       │   ├── memory.high = 1G (Throttle threshold)                    │
│       │   ├── memory.max  = 2G (Hard kill ceiling)                     │
│       │   └─ memory.current (Current usage: 450M)                      │
│       └── pod_analytics/                                               │
│           └── ...                                                      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
When a process executes fork(), its child automatically inherits the parent’s cgroup placement.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
section: Memory Limits, Soft Limits, and Thresholds
text:
Memory Limits, Soft Limits, and Thresholds
In cgroups v2, memory boundaries are governed by four distinct parameters:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        CGROUPS V2 MEMORY THRESHOLDS                    │
│                                                                        │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐     │
│   │ memory.max (Hard Limit - e.g. 2 GiB)                         │     │
│   │ Violations trigger IMMEDIATE synchronous reclaim or OOM KILL │     │
│   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤     │
│   │ memory.high (Soft Throttle - e.g. 1.8 GiB)                   │     │
│   │ Exceeding triggers proactive background reclaim; throttles   │     │
│   │ allocating processes with artificial sleep delays            │     │
│   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤     │
│   │ memory.low (Best-Effort Protection - e.g. 512 MiB)           │     │
│   │ Reclaim avoids taking pages from this cgroup unless all      │     │
│   │ unprotected memory across the system is exhausted            │     │
│   ├──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤     │
│   │ memory.min (Hard Protection - e.g. 256 MiB)                  │     │
│   │ Completely immune to reclaim under ANY circumstance          │     │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

memory.min: Strict guaranteed floor. Pages inside this cgroup will never be reclaimed or swapped out by kernel reclaim loops.
memory.low: Soft protection. Reclaimed only as a last resort.
memory.high: The primary throttling boundary. When usage crosses memory.high, the kernel does not kill the process; it slows down allocating threads by injecting microsecond delays and commands background reclaim to pull memory back under the threshold.
memory.max: The hard absolute ceiling. If usage reaches memory.max and reclaim cannot free enough pages to satisfy the allocation, the kernel triggers an OOM event localized strictly to that cgroup.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
text:
Accounting: Tracking Usage Per-Cgroup
The memory controller charges every allocated page to the cgroup that initiated the allocation:

Anonymous Memory (anon): Process heaps, stacks, and private dirty COW pages.
File Page Cache (file): Cached filesystem pages accessed by processes inside the cgroup.
Kernel Slab Memory (kernel_stack, slab): In cgroups v2, kernel object allocations (such as dentry caches, inode structures, and socket buffers) allocated on behalf of the container are charged directly to the container’s memory usage! An attacker cannot exhaust host RAM by spawning millions of sockets inside a constrained container.

Current usage is inspected via /sys/fs/cgroup/<group>/memory.current and broken down in memory.stat.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
text:
Reclaim Under Constraints: Hierarchical Pressure
When a cgroup crosses its memory.high or memory.max threshold, the kernel initiates Targeted Cgroup Reclaim: - The reclaim engine scans only the LRU lists associated with that specific cgroup and its child slices. - File-backed pages cached by the container are dropped or flushed. - Anonymous pages are compressed into zswap or written to swap. - Surrounding host services and sibling containers experience zero disruption or I/O pressure.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
text:
Swap Accounting and memory.swap Limits
In early cgroups v1, a container with a 1 GiB memory limit could consume 50 GiB of host swap space, degrading entire storage arrays.
cgroups v2 strictly isolates swap through dedicated controls: - memory.swap.max: Sets the absolute maximum swap space the cgroup can occupy. Once reached, anonymous memory cannot be swapped out; further allocations trigger an immediate local OOM event. - Setting memory.swap.max = 0 completely disables swapping for that specific container, ensuring latency-sensitive microservices fail fast rather than stalling on swap I/O.

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
text:
OOM Behavior Within Cgroups
When a container’s memory usage reaches memory.max and reclaim yields zero pages: 1. The kernel’s OOM killer activates, but its scope is confined strictly to tasks within that cgroup. 2. The kernel evaluates oom_score heuristics among processes residing inside the cgroup and selects a victim. 3. The victim process receives SIGKILL. The rest of the host remains completely unaffected. 4. The event is recorded in memory.events: bash    cat /sys/fs/cgroup/docker/container-1/memory.events    # oom 1    # oom_kill 1

title: Chapter 12: Memory Cgroups, Controllers, and Resource Limits
section: Practical Experiment: Setting Up Memory-Limited Containers
text:
Practical Experiment: Setting Up Memory-Limited Containers
We can configure a memory-constrained cgroup using raw systemd or cgroups v2 interfaces:
# 1. Create a transient memory-limited slice using systemd-run
sudo systemd-run --unit=memtest --slice=test.slice \
  --property=MemoryMax=100M \
  --property=MemorySwapMax=0 \
  python3 -c '
data = []
print("Allocating memory...")
for i in range(200):
    data.append(b" " * (1024 * 1024)) # Allocate 1 MiB chunks
    print(f"Allocated {i+1} MiB")
'
Inspect the system journal to observe the localized cgroup containment:
journalctl -u memtest.service -e
Allocating memory...
Allocated 1 MiB
...
Allocated 98 MiB
systemd[1]: memtest.service: A process of this unit was killed by the OOM killer.
systemd[1]: memtest.service: Main process exited, code=killed, status=9/KILL
The process was terminated cleanly at exactly the 100 MiB boundary without causing any memory pressure on the broader host system.

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
text:
Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
When available physical memory is exhausted, all page cache pages have been reclaimed, swap storage is completely full, and memory compaction cannot synthesize a single free block, the operating system enters an existential state: Out of Memory (OOM).
At this juncture, the kernel can no longer service memory allocation requests. If the kernel simply returned -ENOMEM to calling processes, applications would crash haphazardly, and system daemons would hang in undefined deadlock states.
To prevent an uncontrolled system-wide freeze, the Linux kernel deploys its ultimate weapon of last resort: the Out-of-Memory (OOM) Killer.
This chapter explores how the OOM killer selects its victims, the mathematical heuristics behind oom_badness(), how to protect critical daemons using oom_score_adj, kernel panic triggers, automated recovery architectures, and post-mortem incident forensics.

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
section: When Reclaim Fails: The Last Resort
text:
When Reclaim Fails: The Last Resort
The path leading to an OOM kill follows a progressive degradation curve:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        OOM KILLER ESCALATION PATH                      │
│                                                                        │
│   1. Free memory falls below zone WMARK_LOW                            │
│      └─► Background kswapd daemon begins reclaiming clean page cache   │
│                                                                        │
│   2. Free memory falls below zone WMARK_MIN                            │
│      └─► Direct Reclaim: Allocating threads stall; flush dirty pages   │
│                                                                        │
│   3. High-order fragmentation blocks contiguous allocations           │
│      └─► Direct Compaction: Two-pointer scanner attempts page migration│
│                                                                        │
│   4. Swap space reaches 100% saturation; no pages reclaimable          │
│      └─► Kernel invokes out_of_memory() in mm/oom_kill.c               │
│                                                                        │
│   5. The OOM Killer:                                                  │
│      ├─ Evaluates every runnable task on the machine                   │
│      ├─ Computes badness score (0 to 1000)                             │
│      └─ Sends SIGKILL to the single highest-scoring process!           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
section: The OOM Killer Algorithm and Victim Selection

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
text:
Scoring Factors and Heuristics
The badness score is driven by three factors:

Resident Set Size (RSS): Number of physical RAM pages currently mapped into the process’s page tables.
Swap Usage (MM_SWAPENTS): Number of swap slots consumed by the process.
Page Table Overhead (nr_ptes): Memory consumed by the process’s page table structures themselves.
Root Privilege Discount: In older kernels, root-owned processes received a slight discount; modern kernels evaluate strictly based on memory footprint and oom_score_adj.

The task consuming the largest aggregate volume of physical RAM and swap yields the highest score and is selected as the victim.

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
section: OOM Score Adjustment and Task Protection
text:
OOM Score Adjustment and Task Protection
Systems administrators can explicitly bias the OOM killer’s calculations using /proc/[pid]/oom_score_adj:

Range: -1000 to +1000.
-1000 (OOM_SCORE_ADJ_MIN): Makes the process completely immune to the OOM killer. The kernel will never kill this process, even if system memory reaches 100% exhaustion. (Reserved for critical daemons like sshd, kubelet, or hypervisors).
+1000 (OOM_SCORE_ADJ_MAX): Forces the process to be killed first, regardless of how little memory it consumes. (Ideal for batch workers or untrusted sandbox scripts).

# Make SSH daemon completely immune to OOM kill
echo -1000 | sudo tee /proc/$(pgrep -x sshd)/oom_score_adj

# Protect a systemd service declaratively in its unit file
# In /etc/systemd/system/myapp.service:
[Service]
OOMScoreAdjust=-900
To inspect the calculated runtime score of any process:
cat /proc/1234/oom_score

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
text:
System-wide vs Cgroup-local OOM Events

System-wide OOM: Occurs when host physical RAM and swap are completely exhausted. The kernel evaluates all processes across the entire machine.
Cgroup-local OOM: Occurs when a specific container or cgroup reaches its memory.max boundary. The kernel evaluates only tasks belonging to that cgroup, killing an internal process and preserving host stability.

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
section: Kernel Panic Conditions and Memory Exhaustion Scenarios
text:
Kernel Panic Conditions and Memory Exhaustion Scenarios
Under extreme conditions, the OOM killer cannot find a viable victim:

All memory-consuming processes have oom_score_adj = -1000 (immune).
Memory is exhausted entirely within unswappable kernel slab allocations (e.g., driver memory leak).
The kernel parameter vm.panic_on_oom is explicitly enabled:
# /etc/sysctl.d/99-oom.conf
vm.panic_on_oom = 1

When vm.panic_on_oom = 1, the kernel refuses to kill any process and immediately triggers a Kernel Panic, initiating automated hardware reboot via the motherboard watchdog or kdump kernel crash dump.

title: Chapter 13: Out-of-Memory Handling, Panic, and Recovery
section: Real-World Case Studies: OOM Incidents and Post-Mortems
text:
Real-World Case Studies: OOM Incidents and Post-Mortems
When an OOM event occurs in production, the kernel dumps a rich diagnostic trace into the system log (dmesg / journalctl):
sudo dmesg -T | grep -A 20 -B 5 "invoked oom-killer"
[Fri Oct 30 15:20:10 2026] nodejs invoked oom-killer: gfp_mask=0x1100cca(GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE), order=0, oom_score_adj=0
...
[Fri Oct 30 15:20:10 2026] Node 0 active_anon:12401880kB inactive_anon:420kB active_file:12kB inactive_file:8kB unevictable:0kB dirty:0kB writeback:0kB
[Fri Oct 30 15:20:10 2026] Out of memory: Killed process 54201 (worker_task) total-vm:18942000kB, anon-rss:14201880kB, file-rss:0kB, shmem-rss:0kB

Forensic Analysis Checklist

Identify the Trigger vs the Victim: In the trace above, nodejs triggered the allocation that failed, but the victim selected for termination was worker_task (consuming 14.2 GiB). The allocating process is rarely the true cause of the leak.
Inspect active_file vs active_anon: If active_file is near zero, file cache was completely starved prior to the kill.
Verify Swap Saturation: Check if swap space was exhausted or if swapping was disabled.

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
text:
Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
On modern multi-core servers featuring 128, 256, or more physical CPU cores, millions of concurrent allocation, deallocation, page table modification, and cache invalidation operations execute simultaneously every second.
If the Linux kernel relied on a coarse-grained global memory lock, processor cores would spend more than 90% of their execution time stalled on cache coherency traffic and spinlock contention. Conversely, uncoordinated concurrent updates to page tables, freelists, and reference counters would cause catastrophic kernel memory corruption, use-after-free exploits, and silent filesystem destruction.
This chapter examines the synchronization primitives, locking hierarchies, and lockless algorithms that allow the Linux memory management subsystem to scale efficiently across hundreds of cores.

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
section: Concurrency Challenges in a Shared Allocator
text:
Concurrency Challenges in a Shared Allocator
The memory management subsystem faces several acute concurrency challenges:

High Call Frequency: kmalloc, page faults, and page frees occur millions of times per second across all running threads.
Global State Mutation: The buddy allocator maintains global free lists; the page cache maintains global inode mappings; swap maintains shared disk slots.
Cache Line Bouncing: When multiple CPUs contend for the same atomic spinlock or cache line, the inter-core interconnect (UPI on Intel, Infinity Fabric on AMD) is flooded with MESI invalidation traffic.
Deadlock Vulnerability: Memory allocation occurs inside interrupt contexts, page fault handlers, filesystem writeback paths, and storage drivers. A circular lock dependency between memory and I/O will instantly freeze the machine.

┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│             THE LOCK CONTENTION VS MEMORY ISOLATION SPECTRUM           │
│                                                                        │
│ Global Lock (Bottleneck)         Hierarchical / Distributed (Scalable) │
│                                                                        │
│   CPU 0 ──┐                        CPU 0 ──► Per-CPU PCP Array (Fast) │
│   CPU 1 ──┼─► [ Global Lock ]      CPU 1 ──► Per-CPU PCP Array (Fast) │
│   CPU 2 ──┤        │                                   │ (Depleted)    │
│   CPU 3 ──┘   100% Contention                          ▼               │
│               Bus Invalidation                [ Zone Spinlock ]        │
│                                                        │ (Depleted)    │
│                                                        ▼               │
│                                               [ Node pgdat Lock ]      │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
text:
Locking Hierarchy and Deadlock Prevention
To eliminate circular lock deadlocks (ABBA lock inversions), the Linux kernel enforces an unyielding, top-down locking hierarchy across all virtual memory operations:
1. mmap_lock (struct mm_struct) [Down Read / Down Write]
     │
     ▼
2. VMA Lock (struct vm_area_struct) [Per-VMA lock for concurrent faults]
     │
     ▼
3. Page Table Lock (PTL) (pmd_lock / pte_lock) [Spinlock]
     │
     ▼
4. Page Lock (PG_locked flag / folio_lock) [Bit-wait queue]
     │
     ▼
5. Inode i_rwsem & Address Space Lock (i_mapping->i_mmap_rwsem)
     │
     ▼
6. Zone / Node Lock (zone->lock / pgdat->lru_lock) [Spinlock]

The mmap_lock (Formerly mmap_sem)
The mmap_lock is a reader-writer semaphore protecting a process’s virtual address space (mm_struct): - Read Mode (down_read(&mm->mmap_lock)): Multiple threads within the same process handle page faults simultaneously, read /proc/self/maps, or query address mappings. - Write Mode (down_write(&mm->mmap_lock)): Exclusively acquired during mmap(), munmap(), mprotect(), brk(), or mremap(). All page faults across all threads in that process freeze until the structural modification completes.
Historically, heavily multi-threaded workloads (such as JVMs, Go runtimes, and databases) suffered severe latency spikes when background threads called mprotect() or allocated large memory arenas while hundreds of worker threads handled concurrent minor page faults.


Per-VMA Locks (Modern Linux 6.2+)
To break the mmap_lock bottleneck, modern Linux kernels introduce Per-VMA Locking. Each struct vm_area_struct has its own lightweight lock (vma->vm_lock): - A page fault acquires only the local VMA lock in read mode using RCU and sequence counting (vma_start_read(vma)). - Multiple threads can fault on different memory regions (e.g., Thread A on the heap and Thread B on a thread stack) without contending on mm->mmap_lock.

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
section: Zone Locks, pgdat Locks, and LRU Lists
text:
Zone Locks, pgdat Locks, and LRU Lists
Moving from virtual memory to physical memory, the kernel must protect physical frame allocators:

zone->lock: A spinlock protecting the buddy allocator freelists (free_area[order]) within a specific memory zone (e.g., ZONE_NORMAL).
pgdat->lru_lock: Protects the active and inactive LRU lists for an entire NUMA node. When kswapd or direct reclaim scans pages for eviction, it acquires lru_lock.

Because thousands of allocation requests occur per second, threads do not directly acquire zone->lock on every alloc_pages() call. Instead, they hit per-CPU caches.

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
section: Per-CPU Data Structures and Lockless Paths
text:
Per-CPU Data Structures and Lockless Paths
The golden rule of kernel scalability is: The fastest lock is the lock you never acquire.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   PER-CPU PAGE ALLOCATION FAST PATH                     │
│                                                                        │
│   CPU 3 Thread                                                         │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼                                                                  │
│   Disable Preemption / Local Interrupts                                │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ▼                                                                  │
│   Read cpu_id = 3                                                      │
│     │                                                                  │
│     ├───► PCP List has pages?                                          │
│     │       ├── YES: Pop page struct from local array; re-enable IRQ;  │
│     │       │        RETURN (Zero bus locks, zero contention!)         │
│     │       │                                                          │
│     │       └── NO:  Acquire spin_lock(&zone->lock)                    │
│     │                Batch refill 32 pages from Buddy Allocator        │
│     │                Release spin_lock(&zone->lock)                    │
│     │                Pop page; RETURN                                  │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Per-CPU Pagesets (PCP):

Each CPU core maintains a private array of free single pages (struct per_cpu_pages).
Accessing local PCP requires only disabling local interrupts (local_irq_save()) to prevent interrupt handler races. No cross-CPU locks are touched.

SLUB Cpu-Slabs:

kmem_cache_cpu allows lockless fast-path allocations using atomic compare-and-swap (cmpxchg_double) or local freelist traversal.

Page Counter Buffers:

Memory cgroup tracking uses per-CPU stock caches (struct memcg_stock_pcp) to batch charge adjustments, preventing global atomic counter bouncing.

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
section: Diagnosing Scalability Contention on Large Systems
text:
Diagnosing Scalability Contention on Large Systems
Systems engineers can detect memory locking contention in production using built-in Linux profiling tools.

1. Inspecting Spinlock Bottlenecks with perf
# Record lock events and CPU cycles across all cores
sudo perf record -a -g -e lock:lock_acquire,lock:lock_acquired -- sleep 5

# Identify top contended spinlocks
sudo perf report --sort=symbol
If symbols like _raw_spin_lock originating from free_pcppages_bulk, rmqueue_bulk, or lru_lock dominate the profile, the system is suffering from memory allocator lock contention.


2. Monitoring Per-VMA Lock Hit Rates
# Check per-VMA lock statistics on Linux 6.2+
grep -E "vma_lock" /proc/vmstat
Output:
vma_lock_success 184592031
vma_lock_abort   120349
vma_lock_retry   4102
A high ratio of vma_lock_success to vma_lock_abort indicates that page faults are executing concurrently across cores without stalling on mm->mmap_lock.

title: Chapter 14: Synchronization, Concurrency, and Locking in Memory Management
text:
Key Takeaways

Memory allocation relies on a strict lock hierarchy starting with mmap_lock and terminating in zone->lock to prevent circular deadlocks.
Per-VMA locks in modern Linux kernels decouple concurrent page fault handling from global address space modification.
Split page table locks distribute spinlocks to individual PTE and PMD pages, avoiding cross-core collisions.
Per-CPU pagesets and lockless SLUB caches allow over 95% of allocation requests to complete without touching shared bus locks.
RCU and explicit SMP memory barriers ensure fast-path page cache lookups remain coherent across out-of-order CPU microarchitectures.

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
text:
Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
In production environments, memory issues rarely announce themselves with a clear error code. Instead, they manifest as creeping latency degradation, unpredictable tail latency, intermittent CPU spikes caused by background compaction, or sudden out-of-memory crashes that tear down critical microservices.
Taming these behaviors requires an engineering methodology that moves from high-level system metrics down to low-level kernel event tracing and post-mortem crash dump analysis.
This chapter details the tools, kernel instrumentation, and step-by-step diagnostic workflows required to profile, debug, and optimize the Linux virtual memory subsystem.

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
text:
Core Memory Performance Metrics
When diagnosing memory bottlenecks, systems engineers must evaluate five core telemetry dimensions:









Metric Dimension
Key Kernel Counters
Diagnostic Tool
Symptom of Distress




Allocation Latency
pgalloc_normal, allocstall
perf, bpftrace
Slow thread startup, tail latency


Reclaim Pressure
pgscan_direct, pgsteal_kswapd
/proc/vmstat
CPU saturated by kernel reclaimers


TLB Miss Penalty
dtlb_load_misses.walk_duration
perf stat
High cycles per instruction (CPI)


Page Fault Rate
minor_faults, major_faults
pidstat -r, sar -B
Excessive disk reads during faults


Stall Time
some, full memory pressure
/proc/pressure/memory
Direct stalls waiting on RAM/swap

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
text:
Deep /proc and /sys Subsystem Inspection
Before launching dynamic tracers, start by querying the kernel’s built-in accounting files.

1. Granular System Memory: /proc/meminfo
cat /proc/meminfo | grep -E "(MemTotal|MemFree|MemAvailable|Buffers|Cached|Dirty|Writeback|AnonPages|Shmem|Slab|SReclaimable|SUnreclaim|KernelStack|PageTables)"

MemAvailable: The kernel’s estimated quantity of RAM available for starting new applications without swapping.
Dirty vs Writeback: High dirty pages indicate pending disk writeback; if writeback climbs steadily, disk storage bandwidth is saturated.
SReclaimable vs SUnreclaim: Identifies whether SLUB cache footprint can be shrunk under memory pressure.



2. Microscopic VM Counters: /proc/vmstat
# Monitor page allocation stalls and direct reclaim rate in real time
watch -n 1 "grep -E '(allocstall|pgsteal|pgscan|compact)' /proc/vmstat"
allocstall_normal 4891       # Direct allocations stalled waiting on reclaim
pgscan_kswapd     18920114   # Pages scanned by background kswapd
pgscan_direct     2849102    # Pages scanned synchronously by allocating threads
pgsteal_direct    2610481    # Pages successfully reclaimed by direct reclaim
compact_stall     1204       # Threads stalled waiting for page compaction
compact_fail      319        # Compaction attempts that failed
If allocstall or pgscan_direct are increasing rapidly, the system’s memory pressure has escalated past background kswapd into application-blocking direct reclaim.


3. Detailed Per-Process Mapping: /proc/[pid]/smaps_rollup
# Obtain aggregate memory consumption of a process in O(1) time
cat /proc/$(pgrep -o postgres)/smaps_rollup
Output:
Rss:             4194304 kB
Pss:             1842100 kB
Shared_Clean:     819200 kB
Shared_Dirty:    1536000 kB
Private_Clean:         0 kB
Private_Dirty:   1839104 kB
Referenced:      3900000 kB
Anonymous:       1839104 kB
LazyFree:              0 kB
AnonHugePages:    409600 kB
ShmemPmdMapped:        0 kB
FilePmdMapped:         0 kB
Shared_Hugetlb:        0 kB
Private_Hugetlb:       0 kB
Swap:                  0 kB
SwapPss:               0 kB
Locked:                0 kB

Pss (Proportional Set Size): Divides shared memory evenly among all processes sharing the pages. Summing PSS across all processes gives the true total memory footprint without double-counting shared libraries.

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
section: Profiling with perf and Flame Graphs
text:
Profiling with perf and Flame Graphs
Hardware Performance Counters (PMUs) allow you to measure CPU execution stalls caused by memory hierarchy bottlenecks.

Measuring TLB Bottlenecks
# Measure TLB miss overhead during workload execution
sudo perf stat -e dTLB-loads,dTLB-load-misses,iTLB-loads,iTLB-load-misses -p $(pgrep my_app) -- sleep 10
If dTLB-load-misses exceeds 3% of total dTLB-loads, the application’s working set spans too many 4 KiB pages; enabling Transparent Huge Pages (THP) or explicit HugeTLB will recover lost CPU cycles.


Generating Memory Allocation Flame Graphs
# Record kernel stack traces during page allocation events
sudo perf record -a -g -e kmem:mm_page_alloc -- sleep 10

# Generate interactive flame graph using FlameGraph tools
sudo perf script | stackcollapse-perf.pl | flamegraph.pl > page_alloc_flame.svg
In the resulting flame graph, wide plateaus indicate functions that trigger disproportionate numbers of physical page allocations.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   ALLOCATION FLAME GRAPH INTERPRETATION                │
│                                                                        │
│                                                                        │
│                    ┌───────────────────────────────────┐               │
│                    │     do_anonymous_page (PTE Fault) │               │
│                    ├───────────────────────────────────┤               │
│                    │          handle_pte_fault         │               │
│                    ├───────────────────────────────────┤               │
│                    │            __handle_mm_fault      │               │
│                    ├───────────────────────────────────┤               │
│                    │            handle_mm_fault        │               │
│ ┌──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┐ │
│ │                             do_user_addr_fault                     │ │
│ └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│ Wide column = Dominant source of physical memory allocations           │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
text:
Kernel Function Tracing with ftrace
When debugging lock contention or compaction behavior without installing compiler toolchains, the kernel’s built-in ftrace subsystem provides zero-dependency tracing via debugfs.
# Navigate to tracing directory
cd /sys/kernel/tracing

# Reset filters
echo 0 > tracing_on
echo > trace

# Enable function graph tracing on page compaction
echo function_graph > current_tracer
echo compact_zone > set_ftrace_filter

# Start trace, execute test workload, and stop
echo 1 > tracing_on
sleep 1
echo 0 > tracing_on

# Inspect execution call hierarchy with precise function timestamps
head -n 25 trace

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
section: Post-Mortem Crash Dump Analysis with kdump and crash
text:
Post-Mortem Crash Dump Analysis with kdump and crash
When an unrecoverable memory corruption, double-free, or kernel panic occurs, kdump utilizes kexec to boot a secondary “capture kernel” that writes the physical RAM of the crashed system into /var/crash/vmcore.

Analyzing a Memory Panic with crash
# Launch interactive crash analyzer against kernel binary and dump
sudo crash /usr/lib/debug/boot/vmlinux-$(uname -r) /var/crash/2026-10-30/vmcore
Within the crash interactive shell:
crash> bt
# Shows backtrace of the crashing CPU.
# E.g., BUG: unable to handle page fault for address: 0000000000000028
# RIP: 0010:kmem_cache_alloc+0x54/0x2f0

crash> kmem -i
# Displays global kernel memory inventory at the exact instant of crash
                 PAGES        BYTES       PERCENTAGE
    TOTAL MEM  8388608      32.0 GB         ----
         FREE   104201     407.0 MB           1%
         USED  8284407      31.6 GB          98%
       SHARED  2097152       8.0 GB          25%
      BUFFERS    12401      48.4 MB           0%
       CACHED  3145728      12.0 GB          37%
         SLAB  2621440      10.0 GB          31%

crash> kmem -s
# Displays slab allocation breakdown, identifying leaking kmem_cache
CACHE            NAME                 OBJSIZE  ALLOCATED     TOTAL  SLABS  SSIZE
ffff888100032000 kmalloc-512              512    8491024  10000000 625000     8k
ffff888100033000 ext4_inode_cache        1184      41209     50000   1562    32k
If a single cache (like kmalloc-512) consumes 80% of total slabs, examine the active callers using the bt -a command to pinpoint the leaking subsystem.

title: Chapter 15: Performance Optimization, Profiling, and Debugging
text:
The Complete Debugging Workflow
When addressing memory performance regressions in production, adhere to this diagnostic escalation path:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   PRODUCTION VM DEBUGGING ESCALATION                   │
│                                                                        │
│  Level 1: System-Wide Triage                                           │
│  ├─ Check /proc/pressure/memory (Is PSI stall time increasing?)        │
│  ├─ Check /proc/meminfo (Is RAM exhausted? High dirty pages?)          │
│  └─ Check vmstat 1 (Are allocstall or direct reclaim counters firing?) │
│                                                                        │
│  Level 2: Per-Process Profiling                                        │
│  ├─ pidstat -r (Identify fast-growing RSS)                             │
│  ├─ smaps_rollup (Determine PSS vs Anonymous vs File mapping)          │
│  └─ perf stat -e dTLB-load-misses (Detect TLB thrashing)               │
│                                                                        │
│  Level 3: Dynamic Tracing                                              │
│  ├─ bpftrace / BCC memleak (Pinpoint user-space or kernel leaks)       │
│  ├─ perf record -e kmem:mm_page_alloc (Flame graph allocation sources) │
│  └─ ftrace (Analyze compact_zone and kswapd execution chains)          │
│                                                                        │
│  Level 4: Post-Mortem Forensics                                        │
│  └─ crash / kdump (Extract physical slab states, backtraces, registers)│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
Following this structured workflow prevents premature optimization and guides the engineer directly to the root architectural cause.

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
text:
Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
Because virtual memory mediates all hardware execution, operating system privilege levels, and inter-process boundaries, memory management is the primary battleground of modern computer security.
A single memory corruption flaw—whether an out-of-bounds slab write, an uninitialized page read, or a speculative microarchitectural leak—can enable an untrusted user inside a container to break through namespace boundaries, overwrite kernel page tables, and seize total control of physical hardware.
This chapter analyzes the anatomy of memory exploitation techniques, the security mechanisms built into the Linux virtual memory subsystem, hardware-assisted defenses, and kernel compilation flags required to harden production systems.

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
section: Memory Corruption and Kernel Exploitation Primitives
text:
Memory Corruption and Kernel Exploitation Primitives
Kernel memory exploits generally progress through a sequence of classic primitive capabilities:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   EXPLOITATION PRIMITIVE ESCALATION                    │
│                                                                        │
│   Memory Bug (UAF / Slab Overflow / Uninitialized Read)                │
│       │                                                                │
│       ▼                                                                │
│   Arbitrary Memory Read (Defeat KASLR; locate kernel text / creds)     │
│       │                                                                │
│       ▼                                                                │
│   Arbitrary Memory Write (Overwrite task_struct->cred or Page Tables)  │
│       │                                                                │
│       ▼                                                                │
│   Code Execution / Privilege Escalation (UID 0 / Ring 0)               │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Out-of-Bounds (OOB) Write: Writing past the boundary of a buffer allocated via kmalloc().
Use-After-Free (UAF): Accessing a kernel data structure after calling kfree() or kmem_cache_free().
Double Free: Freeing the same memory pointer twice, corrupting allocator freelists.
Type Confusion: Reallocating freed memory with a different object type, tricking the kernel into calling an attacker-controlled function pointer.

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
text:
Use-After-Free (UAF) and Slab-Based Attacks
The SLUB allocator’s predictable object reuse behavior makes it a common target for heap-based exploitation:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                      SLAB HEAP SPRAYING & UAF ATTACK                    │
│                                                                        │
│ Step 1: Object A allocated (contains function pointer ops->execute)    │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│   │ Object A [fd, refcount, *execute_fn = 0xffffffff81203400]        │ │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                        │
│ Step 2: Vulnerability triggers early free of Object A                  │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│   │ Freed Slot on SLUB freelist (Stale pointer still held by victim) │ │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                        │
│ Step 3: Attacker sprays heap with malicious payload of identical size  │
│   ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│   │ Attacker Object [fake_data, *execute_fn = 0xffffffffdeadbeef]    │ │
│   └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                        │
│ Step 4: Victim calls ops->execute(); execution jumps to attacker code! │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Mitigations Against SLUB Attacks
Modern kernels employ several hardening layers in mm/slub.c: - CONFIG_SLAB_FREELIST_HARDENED: Encrypts next-pointers on the freelist using a per-cache random key XORed with the address itself (ptr ^ secret ^ ptr_addr). Overwriting the freelist pointer corrupts the key, triggering a kernel panic rather than arbitrary allocation. - CONFIG_SLAB_FREELIST_RANDOM: Randomizes the order of objects within a slab page during initialization, preventing attackers from predicting adjacent slot offsets. - CONFIG_HARDENED_USERCOPY: Enforces strict bounds checking when copy_to_user() or copy_from_user() transfers data between kernel slabs and user buffers.

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
text:
Information Leaks via Page Reuse
When a physical page is freed back to the buddy allocator by a process containing sensitive data (such as TLS private keys, /etc/shadow contents, or database buffers), that physical frame may subsequently be allocated to an untrusted user process.
If the kernel fails to scrub the page, the new owner can read secrets directly from uninitialized RAM:

Defenses: Page Poisoning and Zeroing

init_on_alloc=1: Enforces that every physical page and SLUB object allocated by the kernel is overwritten with zeroes before being returned to callers.
init_on_free=1: Zeroes memory immediately when freed, erasing secrets and preventing use-after-free data leakage.
Kernel Parameter: Can be toggled at boot time:
# Enable automatic memory zeroing on boot
init_on_alloc=1 init_on_free=1
(Performance impact is typically between 1% and 4% of allocation throughput, but eliminates entire categories of data remanence attacks).

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
section: Address Space Layout Randomization: ASLR and KASLR
text:
Address Space Layout Randomization: ASLR and KASLR
Randomizing memory layouts prevents attackers from hardcoding fixed target addresses in their exploits.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                        KASLR RANDOMIZATION OFFSETS                     │
│                                                                        │
│ Default Virtual Space:                                                 │
│ [ 0xffffffff81000000: Fixed Base ] ────► Predictable payload target    │
│                                                                        │
│ With KASLR Active:                                                     │
│ [ 0xffffffff93400000: Randomized Base ] (Shifted by 64-bit entropy)    │
│                                                                        │
│ Attacker cannot execute Return-Oriented Programming (ROP) gadgets      │
│ without first achieving an Information Disclosure (Info Leak) bug!     │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

User-Space ASLR: Controlled via /proc/sys/kernel/randomize_va_space:

0: Disabled.
1: Conservative (randomizes mmap base, stack, and VDSO).
2: Full (randomizes mmap base, stack, VDSO, and heap brk).

Kernel ASLR (KASLR):

Randomizes the base address of the kernel code section (_text) and the direct physical memory mapping (page_offset_base) during early UEFI/bootloader handoff.
Requires hardware True Random Number Generators (TRNG / RDRAND) or UEFI entropy seeds.

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
section: Hardware-Enforced Protection: SMEP, SMAP, and Canaries
text:
Hardware-Enforced Protection: SMEP, SMAP, and Canaries
Software boundaries are easily bypassed if the CPU hardware does not actively monitor privilege transitions:
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                HARDWARE EXECUTION & ACCESS ENFORCEMENT                 │
│                                                                        │
│  User Space (Ring 3 / EL0)          Kernel Space (Ring 0 / EL1)        │
│  ┌─────────────────────────┐        ┌─────────────────────────┐        │
│  │ User Buffer / Shellcode │        │ Kernel Driver Execution │        │
│  └───────────┬─────────────┘        └────────────┬────────────┘        │
│              │                                   │                     │
│              │ ◄── SMEP Blocks Execution! ───────┤                     │
│              │ (Ring 0 cannot execute Ring 3 code)                     │
│              │                                   │                     │
│              │ ◄── SMAP Blocks Direct Read/Write │                     │
│              │ (Ring 0 cannot read/write Ring 3 memory without stac)   │
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

1. Supervisor Mode Execution Prevention (SMEP / PXN on ARM)

Prevents Ring 0 (kernel mode) from executing instructions residing in user-space pages.
Prevents attackers from redirecting corrupted kernel function pointers directly into user-space shellcode.



2. Supervisor Mode Access Prevention (SMAP / PAN on ARM)

Prevents Ring 0 from reading or writing user-space memory directly.
The kernel can only access user memory within explicit, audited routines (copy_from_user(), copy_to_user()) that temporarily toggle the CPU EFLAGS.AC flag via stac (Set Alignment Check) and clac (Clear Alignment Check) assembly instructions.



3. Stack Canaries (CONFIG_STACKPROTECTOR_STRONG)

Inserts a secret 64-bit random canary value immediately before the return address on the kernel stack frame.
If a stack buffer overflow overwrites the return pointer, the canary is altered; the kernel detects the mismatch upon function return and immediately invokes panic().

title: Chapter 16: Security Implications, Exploits, and Mitigations
section: Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities and TLB Side Channels
text:
Microarchitectural Vulnerabilities and TLB Side Channels
In 2018, the discovery of transient execution vulnerabilities fundamentally reshaped operating system memory design.
┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    SPECULATIVE EXECUTION SIDE CHANNELS                 │
│                                                                        │
│  1. Attacker requests out-of-bounds array access                       │
│  2. CPU branch predictor speculates that bounds check will pass        │
│  3. Secret kernel byte is read into L1 Cache speculatively             │
│  4. Branch misprediction realized; CPU flushes architectural registers │
│  5. BUT: Secret remains in L1 Cache!                                   │
│  6. Attacker measures cache load latency (FLUSH+RELOAD) to infer secret│
└────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Meltdown & Kernel Page Table Isolation (KPTI)

Meltdown (Variant 3): Allowed user-space applications to read kernel memory across the privilege boundary due to speculative out-of-order execution before permission checks completed.
KPTI (Kernel Page Table Isolation): Replaced the shared address space model with dual page tables:

While running in user space, the page tables map only user memory and the minimal trampoline code required to enter the kernel.
While running in kernel space, the full kernel memory map is loaded into CR3.
Trade-off: Every system call requires swapping CR3 and invalidating TLB entries (mitigated partially by PCID hardware support).




Spectre, MDS, and L1TF

Spectre (Variants 1 & 2): Speculative branch target injection and bounds check bypasses. Mitigated via compiler retpolines (CONFIG_RETPOLINE) and speculation barriers (lfence).
MDS (Microarchitectural Data Sampling): Speculatively leaked data from CPU fill buffers and load ports. Mitigated by clearing CPU microarchitectural buffers on user-kernel context switch (mds=full).
